Discrete Beckmann Transport Models
for One-Step Language Modeling and Reasoning

Sophia Tang† Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [    Shiyi Wang Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [
Abstract

Discrete diffusion and flow models are a promising alternative to autoregressive language models, but compressing many-step sampling into fewer steps typically requires distilling a pretrained teacher model. This caps the student at the teacher’s quality and requires a costly two-stage training pipeline. We introduce Discrete Beckmann Transport Models (DBTM), built on a time-independent flow whose autonomous transport map provably carries any point in the ambient space to a fixed point on the vertices of the simplex in a single step. We show that this fixed-point property is characterized by a conservation equation whose residual can be minimized directly from data, removing the requirement for a teacher flow and time conditioning. Under this construction, a partially trained map corresponds to the flow truncated at finite time, so generation reduces to iterating one map until it reaches a fixed point. We further extend the map to a partial-context interpolant where additional function evaluations act as refinement steps rather than ODE integration steps. On language modeling and reasoning tasks, DBTM enables one- and few-step generation that improves quality and accuracy over discrete diffusion and continuous flow baselines.

Correspondence: sophtang@engineering.upenn.edu, fwang@math.harvard.edu

††footnotetext: †Work done while a visiting researcher at Harvard University.

1 Introduction

Discrete diffusion models (Shi et al., 2024; Sahoo et al., 2024; Ou et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025) are competitive alternatives to autoregressive language modeling, offering bidirectional dependencies. However, for sequences of length LL over a vocabulary of size VV, the state space grows as VLV^{L}, forcing practical samplers to factorize the per-step denoising distribution across positions. This factorization discards intra-step dependencies, so unmasking many positions at once degrades sample quality, and high-fidelity generation requires many function evaluations scaling linearly with LL. The resulting limit on parallelism has motivated continuous-space flows that land on the simplex and can be distilled into few-step samplers. Among these techniques are flow maps (Boffi et al., 2025) which have been adapted to discrete sequences (Potaptchik et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026a) by defining a mean denoiser that transports a point at time ss directly to its further denoised state at time tt, landing at a vertex of the simplex at t=1t=1.

A key limitation of few-step language modeling with flow maps is the need to learn both the diagonal (s=ts=t) and off-diagonal (s≠ts\neq t) terms, either by distilling a teacher flow approximating the marginal velocity btb_{t} or by training both jointly via bootstrapping, with the former commonly performing better (Potaptchik et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026a). Distillation caps the student at the teacher’s quality, propagating its approximation errors, and imposes a two-stage pipeline that must train the teacher to convergence before fitting the student. Bootstrapping removes the teacher but makes the off-diagonal targets depend on the model’s own evolving predictions, which can be unstable and slow to converge.

We introduce Discrete Beckmann Transport Models (DBTM), a framework that learns the autonomous transport map TT associated with the time-independent flow, which provably has straighter trajectories than the time-dependent flow and carries any ambient point to the data manifold supported on the simplex vertices. This fixed-point property is formalized by the conservation equation b⋅∇T=0b\cdot\nabla T=0, whose residual we minimize to train directly from data, replacing the distillation stage entirely.

Our main contributions can be summarized as follows:

  1. 1.

    Discrete Beckmann Transport Models: From the time-independent flow ODE Xs​(x0)X_{s}(x_{0}), we define a one-step map T​(x):=Xτ⁡(x0)​(x)T(x):=X_{\tau(x_{0})}(x) that provably transports any ambient point to a fixed point on the discrete data manifold without conditioning on time.

  2. 2.

    Direct Training from Data: TT can be trained without distillation by iteratively regressing onto a frozen copy of itself plus an Euler correction. A partially trained TθT_{\theta} maps to an intermediate point along the autonomous flow and converges to Tθ⋆=Xτ⁡(x0)T_{\theta^{\star}}=X_{\tau(x_{0})}, so the manifold can be reached by iteratively applying TθT_{\theta}.

  3. 3.

    Self-Correction via Iterative Refinement: We train with a partial-context interpolant, which enables confidence- or quality-based iterative refinement during training and inference.

We validate DBTM on unconditional language modeling and conditional reasoning tasks, demonstrating stronger performance than baselines at lower or matched NFEs. Further discussion of related works is provided in App. 9.

2 Preliminaries

Continuous Generative Modeling on the Simplex

Let 𝒱={1,…,V}\mathcal{V}=\{1,\dots,V\} be a vocabulary and x=(x1,…,xL)∈𝒱Lx=(x^{1},\dots,x^{L})\in\mathcal{V}^{L} a sequence of LL tokens. Embedding each token as a vertex of the probability simplex ΔV−1:={x∈ℝ≥0V:∑jxj=1}\Delta^{V-1}:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{V}_{\geq 0}:\sum_{j}x_{j}=1\} via the one-hot map xℓ↦exℓx^{\ell}\mapsto e_{x^{\ell}} represents a sequence with a point in (ℝV)L(\mathbb{R}^{V})^{L}. The data distribution μ1\mu_{1} is atomic, supported on the VLV^{L} vertex configurations:

M1:={e1,…,eV}L⊂(ΔV−1)L,\displaystyle M_{1}:=\{e_{1},\dots,e_{V}\}^{L}\subset(\Delta^{V-1})^{L}, (1)

and we decode by taking the per-position argmax x↦(arg⁡maxj⁡xjℓ)ℓ∈[L]x\mapsto(\arg\max_{j}x^{\ell}_{j})_{\ell\in[L]}, which is exact on M1M_{1}. The prior distribution can be defined as a product of Gaussians μ0=𝒩​(0,σ2​𝑰V)⊗L\mu_{0}=\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}\bm{I}_{V})^{\otimes L}, and continuous generative modeling aims to transport μ0\mu_{0} to μ1\mu_{1} via a continuous flow in ambient space.

Generative Flows and Flow Maps

The stochastic interpolants framework (Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2023; Albergo et al., 2025) connects μ0\mu_{0} and μ1\mu_{1} through the interpolant:

It:=αt​x0+βt​x1,t∈[0,1]\displaystyle I_{t}:=\alpha_{t}x_{0}+\beta_{t}x_{1},\quad t\in[0,1] (2)

with x0∼μ0x_{0}\sim\mu_{0}, x1∼μ1x_{1}\sim\mu_{1} independent and schedules satisfying α0=β1=1\alpha_{0}=\beta_{1}=1, α1=β0=0\alpha_{1}=\beta_{0}=0, so that I0=x0I_{0}=x_{0} and I1=x1I_{1}=x_{1}. We take βt=1−αt\beta_{t}=1-\alpha_{t} with αt=(1−t)a\alpha_{t}=(1-t)^{a} for a≥1a\geq 1, recovering the linear interpolant at a=1a=1. Writing μt:=Law⁡(It)\mu_{t}:=\mathrm{Law}(I_{t}), the flow matching velocity is given by:

bt​(x):=𝔼x0,x1​[I˙t|It=x]=arg⁡minb^t​𝔼x0,x1​[|b^t​(It)−I˙t|2]\displaystyle b_{t}(x):=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0},x_{1}}\left[\dot{I}_{t}\big|I_{t}=x\right]=\underset{\hat{b}_{t}}{\arg\min}\ \mathbb{E}_{x_{0},x_{1}}\left[\left|\hat{b}_{t}(I_{t})-\dot{I}_{t}\right|^{2}\right] (3)

where the second equality is the regression characterization that makes btb_{t} learnable from samples without access to μt\mu_{t}. The pair (bt,μt)(b_{t},\mu_{t}) satisfies the continuity equation:

∇⋅(btμt)=−∂tμt.\displaystyle\nabla\cdot(b_{t}\mu_{t})=-\partial_{t}\mu_{t}. (4)

The probability flow ODE is given by:

dd​t​Xs,t​(x)=bt​(Xs,t​(x)),Xs,s​(x)=x\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}X_{s,t}(x)=b_{t}(X_{s,t}(x)),\quad X_{s,s}(x)=x (5)

transports μs\mu_{s} to μt\mu_{t}. Sampling from a learned btb_{t} requires integrating (5), at a cost measured in network function evaluations (NFE). Flow maps instead learn the two-time solution operator Xs,tX_{s,t}, advancing the state over a finite interval in one evaluation. By uniqueness of the ODE solution, it obeys the semigroup property:

Xt,u∘Xs,t=Xs,ufor all​s≤t≤u,Xs∘Xu=Xs+uwhen​bt≡b\displaystyle X_{t,u}\circ X_{s,t}=X_{s,u}\ \ \text{for all}\ s\leq t\leq u,\qquad X_{s}\circ X_{u}=X_{s+u}\ \ \text{when}\ b_{t}\equiv b (6)

where the second identity is the case where the velocity field is time-independent.

3 Autonomous Flows on the Simplex

3.1 Properties of the Autonomous Flow

While standard flow matching learns a time-dependent field btb_{t} and integrates it over a fixed horizon t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], an autonomous flow model (Lee et al., 2026b) defines a time-independent velocity field bb:

b⁡(x):=𝔼t,x0,x1​[I˙t|It=x]=arg⁡minb^​𝔼t,x0,x1​[|b^​(It)−I˙t|2],t∼𝒰⁡[0,1]\displaystyle b(x):=\mathbb{E}_{t,x_{0},x_{1}}[\dot{I}_{t}|I_{t}=x]=\underset{\hat{b}}{\arg\min}\mathbb{E}_{t,x_{0},x_{1}}\left[|\hat{b}(I_{t})-\dot{I}_{t}|^{2}\right],\qquad t\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1] (7)

associated with the autonomous ODE:

X˙s​(x0)=b⁡(Xs​(x0)),X0​(x0)=x0\displaystyle\dot{X}_{s}(x_{0})=b(X_{s}(x_{0})),\quad X_{0}(x_{0})=x_{0} (8)

where s∈[0,∞)s\in[0,\infty) is the integration time of the autonomous ODE, which is decoupled from the interpolation time tt.

Proposition 3.1 (Time-average of standard flow matching).

Given the time-dependent flow matching velocity bt​(x):=𝔼x0,x1​[I˙t|It=x]b_{t}(x):=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0},x_{1}}[\dot{I}_{t}|I_{t}=x] defined with the interpolant It:=αt​x0+βt​x1I_{t}:=\alpha_{t}x_{0}+\beta_{t}x_{1}, the autonomous velocity field is the time-weighted average:

b⁡(x)\displaystyle b(x) =∫01μt​(x)​bt​(x)​𝑑t∫01μt​(x)​𝑑t\displaystyle=\frac{\int_{0}^{1}\mu_{t}(x)b_{t}(x)dt}{\int_{0}^{1}\mu_{t}(x)dt} (9)

The proof is in App. 11.1.1. Intuitively, b⁡(x)b(x) averages the velocities of every interpolant passing through xx at any time t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], so the field depends on position alone, removing the time dependence that constrains the flow to terminate at μ1\mu_{1} at t=1t=1 and yielding straighter dynamics. We make this precise in App. 11.1. Just as the time-dependent flow satisfies a continuity equation (4), the autonomous flow satisfies the divergence condition (Proof in App. 10.2) (Lee et al., 2026b) obtained by integrating over time t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1]:

∫01∇⋅(btμt)=−∫01∂tpt⟹∇⋅j=μ0−μ1\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\nabla\cdot(b_{t}\mu_{t})=-\int_{0}^{1}\partial_{t}p_{t}\implies\nabla\cdot j=\mu_{0}-\mu_{1} (10)

where j=ν​b=∫01μt​bt​𝑑tj=\nu b=\int_{0}^{1}\mu_{t}b_{t}dt is the current and ν⁡(x):=∫01μt​(x)​𝑑t\nu(x):=\int_{0}^{1}\mu_{t}(x)dt the occupation measure. This makes μ0\mu_{0} the source and μ1\mu_{1} the sink of the current, so bb transports μ0\mu_{0} to μ1\mu_{1} – with the key distinction that XsX_{s} need not reach M1M_{1} at s=1s=1. We call the time at which it converges to M1M_{1} the hitting time τ(x0)∈[0,+∞)\tau(x_{0})\in[0,+\infty), and show it is finite on the simplex.

Theorem 3.1 (Convergence of autonomous flow on the simplex).

Let μ0\mu_{0} be absolutely continuous on (ℝV)L(\mathbb{R}^{V})^{L} with continuous, strictly positive density, and let

M1=supp⁡(μ1)=({e1,…,eV})L⊂(ΔV−1)L\displaystyle M_{1}=\mathrm{supp}(\mu_{1})=(\{e_{1},\dots,e_{V}\})^{L}\subset(\Delta^{V-1})^{L} (11)

be the finite set of VLV^{L} vertex configurations. Then for μ0\mu_{0}-a.e. x0x_{0}, the autonomous flow Xs​(x0)X_{s}(x_{0}) satisfies:

  1. (i)

    Absorption: if Xs⋆​(x0)∈M1X_{s^{\star}}(x_{0})\in M_{1} for some s⋆<∞s^{\star}<\infty, then Xs​(x0)=Xs⋆​(x0)X_{s}(x_{0})=X_{s^{\star}}(x_{0}) for all s>s⋆s>s^{\star}.

  2. (ii)

    Convergence: there is x⋆​(x0)∈M1x^{\star}(x_{0})\in M_{1} with lims→∞Xs​(x0)=x⋆​(x0)\lim_{s\to\infty}X_{s}(x_{0})=x^{\star}(x_{0}).

  3. (iii)

    Finite hitting time: for the linear interpolant It=(1−t)​x0+t​x1I_{t}=(1-t)x_{0}+tx_{1}, τ⁡(x0):=inf{t≥0:Xs​(x0)∈M1}<+∞\tau(x_{0}):=\inf\{t\geq 0:X_{s}(x_{0})\in M_{1}\}<+\infty. Although the autonomous velocity field vanishes at the vertices, b⁡(ej)=0b(e_{j})=0 for all ej∈M1e_{j}\in M_{1}, it does not vanish in the limit approaching them: limr↓0b⁡(ej+r​ω)=−κ⁡(ω)​ω\lim_{r\downarrow 0}b(e_{j}+r\omega)=-\kappa(\omega)\omega. The approach speed is bounded below by κ−>0\kappa_{-}>0 and τ⁡(x0)≤tentry+2​r1/κ−\tau(x_{0})\leq t_{\text{entry}}+2r_{1}/\kappa_{-} for a fixed radius r1r_{1}.

The proof is in App. 11.4. The resulting discontinuity in bb at the vertices is an artifact of the linear interpolant: for a general interpolant (2) that is self-stopping, i.e., α˙t→0\dot{\alpha}_{t}\to 0 as t→1t\to 1, Proposition 11.5 shows bb is continuous at the vertices with b⁡(x)→0b(x)\to 0 as x→eix\to e_{i}.

3.2 Autonomous Transport Map

Given the hitting time τ⁡(x0)\tau(x_{0}) of the autonomous flow Xs​(x0)X_{s}(x_{0}), the associated one-step transport map TT can be written as the limit:

T⁡(x0):=lims→τ⁡(x0)Xs​(x0)∈M1,T#​μ0=μ1\displaystyle T(x_{0}):=\lim_{s\to\tau(x_{0})}X_{s}(x_{0})\in M_{1},\quad T_{\#}\mu_{0}=\mu_{1} (12)

which is also the pushforward of μ0\mu_{0} to μ1\mu_{1}. Since Xs​(x0)X_{s}(x_{0}) is a deterministic function of x0x_{0}, starting along any point Xs​(x0)X_{s}(x_{0}) for s∈[0,τ⁡(x0))s\in[0,\tau(x_{0})) yields the same fixed point T⁡(Xs​(x0))=T⁡(x0)T(X_{s}(x_{0}))=T(x_{0}). By the semigroup condition (6), the map TT is idempotent such that T∘k​(⋅)=T∘k′​(⋅)T^{\circ k}(\cdot)=T^{\circ k^{\prime}}(\cdot) for any k,k′∈ℕk,k^{\prime}\in\mathbb{N}.

Proposition 3.2 (Autonomous transport map solves conservation equation (Lee et al., 2026b)).

Given the autonomous flow velocity field bb, the autonomous flow Xs​(x0)X_{s}(x_{0}) defined in (8) solves the Eulerian equation:

{b⁡(x)⋅∇Xs​(x)=∂sXs​(x),X0​(x)=xx∉M1Xs​(x)=xx∈M1\displaystyle\begin{cases}b(x)\cdot\nabla X_{s}(x)=\partial_{s}X_{s}(x),\quad X_{0}(x)=x&x\notin M_{1}\\ X_{s}(x)=x&x\in M_{1}\end{cases} (13)

Since the autonomous transport map T⁡(x)T(x) defined in (12) is the limit of Xs​(x)X_{s}(x) as s→τ⁡(x)s\to\tau(x) with vanishing velocity at the vertices (X˙s​(ej)=0\dot{X}_{s}(e_{j})=0 for all j∈{1,…,V}j\in\{1,\dots,V\}) by Theorem 3.1, T⁡(x)T(x) is the unique solution of the conservation equation:

{b​(x)⋅∇T​(x)=0x∉M1T⁡(x)=xx∈M1\displaystyle\begin{cases}b(x)\cdot\nabla T(x)=0&x\notin M_{1}\\ T(x)=x&x\in M_{1}\end{cases} (14)

Proposition 3.2 follows from Theorem 3.1, with proof in App. 11.6. This is the key result that drives a principled approach for training the one-step map directly from data without distillation.

4 Learning One-Step Maps Without Distillation

We present a method of directly learning the one-step transport map TT by matching the updates that converge to the solution of the conservation equation in (14). The converged map TT transports any noisy state to its corresponding fixed point on the data manifold, yielding one-step generation and principled refinement techniques.

4.1 Iteratively Solving the Eulerian Equation

Unlike previous few-step model training, which requires distillation or bootstrapping from an approximated target, Proposition 3.2 presents a principled approach to learning TT by iteratively regressing the autonomous flow Xs​(x)X_{s}(x) until the equilibrium point when b⁡(x)⋅∇Xτ⁡(x)​(x)=b⁡(x)⋅∇T​(x)=0b(x)\cdot\nabla X_{\tau(x)}(x)=b(x)\cdot\nabla T(x)=0 for all x∈(ℝV)Lx\in(\mathbb{R}^{V})^{L}. Starting from an untrained map T(0)​(x)=X(0)​(x)=xT^{(0)}(x)=X^{(0)}(x)=x, we iteratively regress the Euler step of size η\eta:

X(n+1)​(x)=X(n)​(x)+η​b​(x)⋅∇X(n)​(x)\displaystyle X^{(n+1)}(x)=X^{(n)}(x)+\eta b(x)\cdot\nabla X^{(n)}(x) (15)

where TθT_{\theta} is trained to match X(n+1)X^{(n+1)} given fixed X(n)X^{(n)} as X(n)→TX^{(n)}\to T for large nn. Since we define b⁡(x):=𝔼t,x0,x1​[I˙t|It=x]b(x):=\mathbb{E}_{t,x_{0},x_{1}}[\dot{I}_{t}|I_{t}=x], the optimal map is:

T=arg⁡minTθ​𝔼t,x0,x1​[‖Tθ​(It)−sg​(Tθ​(It)+I˙t⋅∇Tθ​(It))‖2]\displaystyle T=\underset{T_{\theta}}{\arg\min}\mathbb{E}_{t,x_{0},x_{1}}\left[\|T_{\theta}(I_{t})-\text{sg}(T_{\theta}(I_{t})+\dot{I}_{t}\cdot\nabla T_{\theta}(I_{t}))\|^{2}\right] (16)

minimized exactly when TT satisfies the conservation equation 𝔼t,x0,x1​[I˙t⋅∇Tθ​(It)|It=x]=b⁡(x)⋅∇Tθ​(x)=0\mathbb{E}_{t,x_{0},x_{1}}[\dot{I}_{t}\cdot\nabla T_{\theta}(I_{t})|I_{t}=x]=b(x)\cdot\nabla T_{\theta}(x)=0. Crucially, this objective ensures that even when TθT_{\theta} has not converged, it approximates a map to some point along XsX_{s}, so by the semigroup property (6), kk inference-time iterations Tθ∘k​(x0)T_{\theta}^{\circ k}(x_{0}) approximates along the flow to Xk​t​(x0)X_{kt}(x_{0}), which converges to M1M_{1} as k​t→τ⁡(x0)kt\to\tau(x_{0}).

4.2 Training Objectives for the Transport Map

In practice, the autonomous transport map is parameterized as Tθ​(⋅)=softmax​(fθ​(⋅))T_{\theta}(\cdot)=\text{softmax}(f_{\theta}(\cdot)) for a neural network fθf_{\theta}. Since the map is restricted to the simplex, we formulate each objective as a cross-entropy (CE) over categorical distributions rather than an unconstrained squared error, with the exception of the transport loss where the target does not lie on the simplex.

Transport Loss

From (16), the transport loss is obtained by regressing TθT_{\theta} onto the stop-gradient of itself, added to the Euler step correction along the autonomous flow:

ℒtransport​(θ):=𝔼t,x0,x1​[∑ℓ∈[L]∖𝒞‖Tθ​(It)ℓ−sg​(Tθ​(It)+I˙t⋅∇Tθ​(It))ℓ‖2]\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{transport}}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{t,x_{0},x_{1}}\bigg[\sum_{\ell\in[L]\setminus\mathcal{C}}\left\|T_{\theta}(I_{t})_{\ell}-\text{sg}(T_{\theta}(I_{t})+\dot{I}_{t}\cdot\nabla T_{\theta}(I_{t}))_{\ell}\right\|^{2}\bigg] (17)

where 𝒞\mathcal{C} is the set of committed tokens and the correction dd​t​T​(It)=I˙t⋅∇T​(It)\tfrac{d}{dt}T(I_{t})=\dot{I}_{t}\cdot\nabla T(I_{t}) is tangent to the simplex and its elements sum to zero.

Semigroup Loss

From (12), we show that by the semigroup condition Tθ∘k​(⋅)=Tθ∘k′​(⋅)T_{\theta}^{\circ k}(\cdot)=T_{\theta}^{\circ k^{\prime}}(\cdot), which we enforce using the semigroup loss:

ℒsemi​(θ):=𝔼t,x0,x1​[∑k∈𝒦∑ℓ∈[L]∖𝒞CE​(Tθ​(It)ℓ,sg​(Tθ∘k​(It)ℓ))]\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{semi}}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{t,x_{0},x_{1}}\bigg[\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}\sum_{\ell\in[L]\setminus\mathcal{C}}\text{CE}\left(T_{\theta}(I_{t})_{\ell},\text{sg}(T^{\circ k}_{\theta}(I_{t})_{\ell})\right)\bigg] (18)

for k∈𝒦⊂ℕk\in\mathcal{K}\subset\mathbb{N} applications of the map. We apply this loss only toward the end of training, since the initial identity map T=idT=\text{id} satisfies it trivially.

Boundary Loss

To enforce the boundary condition T⁡(x)=xT(x)=x for x∈M1x\in M_{1} from Proposition 3.2, we add a boundary loss:

ℒbnd​(θ):=𝔼x1​[∑ℓ∈[L]∖𝒞CE​(Tθ​(x1)ℓ,x1ℓ)]\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{bnd}}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{x_{1}}\bigg[\sum_{\ell\in[L]\setminus\mathcal{C}}\text{CE}\left(T_{\theta}(x_{1})_{\ell},x_{1}^{\ell}\right)\bigg] (19)

Beyond the boundary itself, any intermediate ItI_{t} should map to its target, Tθ​(It)=x1T_{\theta}(I_{t})=x_{1}. While the anchor condition is implicitly enforced by the transport loss, the geometry of the simplex makes explicit enforcement useful over a specific time interval, which we describe next.

4.3 Phase Transitions and the Anchor Loss

The flow constructed from the time-dependent interpolant on the simplex commits to a vertex at a short time window called the phase transition. Before the transition, the output token remains uncertain; after it, the token is committed, and further integration does not change the output. Such transitions have been analyzed in diffusion models (Ambrogioni, 2025; Yu and Huang, 2025), and we can use tools from random energy models (REM) (Derrida, 1980) to determine the timing of this transition.

Theorem 4.1 (Phase Transition and Commitment Time).

The phase transition where the interpolant (2) commits to a vertex occurs at time:

t⋆=1−(1+σ2​log⁡V)−1/a\displaystyle t^{\star}=1-\left(1+\sigma\sqrt{2\log V}\right)^{-1/a} (20)

where σ\sigma is the noise scale of the x0x_{0}, and aa is the exponent on αt=(1−t)a\alpha_{t}=(1-t)^{a} and VV is the vocabulary size defining the simplex ΔV−1\Delta^{V-1}.

The full derivation is in App. 11.2. The derivation relies on the idea that competing forces pull the flow trajectory towards each of the VV vertices, resembling the selection of states in a random energy model at a given temperature, which undergoes a phase transition at t=t⋆t=t^{\star}. With the target vertex fixed at eke_{k} during training, the trajectory starts from x0x_{0}, where each vertex carries an energy proportional to the noise scale σ\sigma, and the flow commits to the target when the energy of the target vertex outweighs the competing energies of all other vertices j≠kj\neq k. Intuitively, this means that the interval [0,t⋆][0,t^{\star}] is when the flow must resolve uncertainty in coordination with the other positions, and the interval [t⋆,1][t^{\star},1] is the period post-transition where the endpoint is decided, and we can safely anchor the trajectory to the dominant vertex.

This gives a principled criterion for when to supervise the map toward its target. Over [t⋆,1][t^{\star},1], where the endpoint is already decided, we can anchor Tθ​(It)T_{\theta}(I_{t}) directly without sacrificing diversity:

ℒanchor(θ):=𝔼t,x0,x1[∑ℓ𝟏[t>tanchor]CE(Tθ(It)ℓ,x1ℓ)]\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{anchor}}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{t,x_{0},x_{1}}\bigg[\sum_{\ell}\bm{1}[t>t_{\text{anchor}}]\text{CE}\left(T_{\theta}(I_{t})^{\ell},x_{1}^{\ell}\right)\bigg] (21)

with tanchor=t⋆t_{\text{anchor}}=t^{\star}. Empirically, disabling ℒanchor\mathcal{L}_{\text{anchor}} or setting tanchor>t⋆t_{\text{anchor}}>t^{\star} slowed convergence, while tanchor<t⋆t_{\text{anchor}}<t^{\star} caused mode collapse (Table 12). More broadly, this characterization of the commitment time on the simplex suggests that the transport loss (17) and inference-time steering are best concentrated on the pre-transition interval [0,t⋆][0,t^{\star}], where the endpoint is still being resolved.

5 Training and Sampling with Fixed-Point Refinement

5.1 Test-Time Scaling with Self-Refinement

Partial-Context Interpolant

We consider the subclass of interpolants in which tokens at positions 𝒞⊂{1,…,L}\mathcal{C}\subset\{1,\dots,L\} in the sequence are held as context tokens in their clean state Itℓ=x1ℓI^{\ell}_{t}=x^{\ell}_{1}, while the remaining are noised to time tt:

Itℓ​(𝒞):={x1ℓℓ∈𝒞αtℓ​x0ℓ+(1−αtℓ)​x1ℓℓ∈[L]∖𝒞\displaystyle I_{t}^{\ell}(\mathcal{C}):=\begin{cases}x_{1}^{\ell}&\ell\in\mathcal{C}\\ \alpha_{t}^{\ell}x_{0}^{\ell}+(1-\alpha_{t}^{\ell})x_{1}^{\ell}&\ell\in[L]\setminus\mathcal{C}\end{cases} (22)

The map TθT_{\theta} remains time-independent but is trained on this larger family of per-position interpolants Itℓ​(𝒞)I_{t}^{\ell}(\mathcal{C}), enabling conditioning on partial clean contexts during inference.

Confidence-Based Refinement

Using the predicted map TθT_{\theta}, we can obtain a measure of the model’s per-token confidence qϕℓq_{\phi}^{\ell} and use it to determine which tokens to renoise and refine via the context-dependent map. Concretely, we define:

qℓ​(Tθ​(x)):=⟨Tθ​(x),x^1⟩,x^1=arg⁡max⁡(Tθ​(x))\displaystyle q^{\ell}(T_{\theta}(x)):=\langle T_{\theta}(x),\hat{x}_{1}\rangle,\quad\hat{x}_{1}=\arg\max(T_{\theta}(x)) (23)

Given a threshold κ\kappa (e.g. κ=0.9\kappa=0.9), the refinement step holds the clean one-hot tokens x^ℓ\hat{x}^{\ell} for the set of high-confidence positions 𝒞:={ℓ:qℓ​(Tθ​(x))≥κ}\mathcal{C}:=\{\ell:q^{\ell}(T_{\theta}(x))\geq\kappa\} and samples fresh noise for all remaining positions ℓ∈[L]∖𝒞\ell\in[L]\setminus\mathcal{C}, and reapplies the map TθT_{\theta}, which training with the partial-context interpolant makes well-defined.

Refinement with Learned Per-Token Quality

Another approach to performing self-correction on the output of the transport map is to measure the coherence of each token given the predicted context and resampling noise for incoherent predictions. The ideal coherence score is the probability of the proposed token x^1ℓ\hat{x}^{\ell}_{1} given the ground truth at all other positions, q⋆ℓ​(x^):=Pr​[x^ℓ∣x1⊕mℓ]q_{\star}^{\ell}(\hat{x}):=\text{Pr}[\hat{x}^{\ell}\mid x_{1}\oplus m^{\ell}], where mℓm^{\ell} masks the ℓ\ellth position. Since x1x_{1} is unavailable at inference, computing it would cost LL extra forward passes. Following Kim et al. (2026), we replace the ground truth with the model’s own prediction and define the per-token quality:

qϕℓ​(Tθ​(x))=Pr​[x^1ℓ=x1ℓ∣Tθ​(x)],x^ℓ=arg⁡max⁡(Tθ​(x)ℓ)\displaystyle q^{\ell}_{\phi}(T_{\theta}(x))=\text{Pr}\left[\hat{x}^{\ell}_{1}=x_{1}^{\ell}\mid T_{\theta}(x)\right],\quad\hat{x}^{\ell}=\arg\max\left(T_{\theta}(x)^{\ell}\right) (24)

which can be estimated by a learnable quality head with parameters ϕ\phi trained by minimizing:

ℒϕ(ϕ)=𝔼x0,x1[∑ℓBCE(𝟏[x^1ℓ=x1ℓ],qϕℓ(Tθ(x)))],x^1=argmax(Tθ(x))\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\phi}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0},x_{1}}\bigg[\sum_{\ell}\text{BCE}\left(\bm{1}[\hat{x}_{1}^{\ell}=x_{1}^{\ell}],q_{\phi}^{\ell}(T_{\theta}(x))\right)\bigg],\quad\hat{x}_{1}=\arg\max\left(T_{\theta}(x)\right) (25)

Since this expectation is over the same (x0,x1)(x_{0},x_{1}) pairs as the map objectives, it trains jointly with TθT_{\theta}. At inference, obtaining qϕq_{\phi} costs no additional NFE and defines 𝒞:={ℓ:qϕℓ​(Tθ​(x))≥κ}\mathcal{C}:=\{\ell:q_{\phi}^{\ell}(T_{\theta}(x))\geq\kappa\} just like confidence-based refinement. Algorithm 2 provides the full inference algorithm with refinement.

5.2 Training with Refinement in the Loop

Both refinement rules reuse a map trained on the partial-context interpolant of Section 5.1, where the context set 𝒞\mathcal{C} is drawn at random. At inference, however, 𝒞\mathcal{C} is not random. It is built up over rounds by committing the highest-confidence or quality positions first. The training distribution therefore contains out-of-distribution contexts, since none of the losses enforce the map to complete the structured context generated from the inference sampler. The mismatch is significant in the few-NFE regime: under a budget of kk rounds, each round commits roughly 1/k1/k of the remaining positions, so the context after round rr is a large, highly non-uniform set, and qϕq_{\phi} is also out of distribution when scoring it.

Commit Rule

We close this gap by supervising TθT_{\theta} on the commit sets the sampler is likely to visit at inference. Index refinement rounds by r=1,…,kr=1,\dots,k with 𝒞0=∅\mathcal{C}_{0}=\emptyset, and let ℛr:=[L]∖𝒞r−1\mathcal{R}_{r}:=[L]\setminus\mathcal{C}_{r-1} be the positions still uncommitted entering round rr. Writing qℓq^{\ell} for the commit score of position ℓ\ell (confidence or the quality qϕℓq_{\phi}^{\ell}), each round commits the set Δ​𝒞r\Delta\mathcal{C}_{r} ranked highest by qℓq^{\ell} and renoises the rest:

Δ𝒞r:={ℓ∈ℛr:qℓ≥κ}⏟threshold∪topnr⁡(ℛr,q)⏟floor,nr:=⌈|ℛr|k−r+1⌉,x^r,kℓ:={x1ℓℓ∈𝒞rx0ℓℓ∈[L]∖𝒞r\displaystyle\Delta\mathcal{C}_{r}:=\underbrace{\{\ell\in\mathcal{R}_{r}:q^{\ell}\geq\kappa\}}_{\text{threshold}}\;\cup\;\underbrace{\operatorname{top}_{n_{r}}\big(\mathcal{R}_{r};q\big)}_{\text{floor}},\qquad n_{r}:=\Big\lceil\tfrac{|\mathcal{R}_{r}|}{k-r+1}\Big\rceil,\qquad\hat{x}_{r,k}^{\ell}:=\begin{cases}x_{1}^{\ell}&\ell\in\mathcal{C}_{r}\\ x_{0}^{\ell}&\ell\in[L]\setminus\mathcal{C}_{r}\end{cases} (26)

where topnr⁡(ℛr,q)\operatorname{top}_{n_{r}}(\mathcal{R}_{r};q) denotes the nrn_{r} highest-scoring positions of ℛr\mathcal{R}_{r}, and 𝒞r:=𝒞r−1∪Δ​𝒞r\mathcal{C}_{r}:=\mathcal{C}_{r-1}\cup\Delta\mathcal{C}_{r}. So every position above κ\kappa is committed, and at minimum nrn_{r} positions are committed regardless. Since |Δ​𝒞r|≥nr|\Delta\mathcal{C}_{r}|\geq n_{r} and nk=|ℛk|n_{k}=|\mathcal{R}_{k}|, we have 𝒞k=[L]\mathcal{C}_{k}=[L] and the sampler always terminates within kk NFE.

Refinement-in-Loop Objective

From (26), x^r,k:=Renoise​(Tθ​(x^r−1,k))\hat{x}_{r,k}:=\textsc{Renoise}(T_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{r-1,k})) can be used like the partial-context interpolant of Section 5.1 with the committed positions determined from sampling with refinement. We train the map to recover x1x_{1} from these states via the refinement-in-loop (ril) objective:

ℒril-c​(θ):=𝔼x0,x1​[∑k∈𝒦∑r=1k∑ℓ∈[L]∖𝒞rCE​(Tθ​(x^r−1,k)ℓ,x1ℓ)]\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{ril-c}}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0},x_{1}}\bigg[\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}\sum_{r=1}^{k}\sum_{\ell\in[L]\setminus\mathcal{C}_{r}}\text{CE}\left(T_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{r-1,k})^{\ell},\ x_{1}^{\ell}\right)\bigg] (27)

which sums only over uncommitted positions, since the committed positions are pinned one-hot and carry no gradient. The same states are used to train the quality head:

ℒril-​ϕ(ϕ):=𝔼x0,x1[∑k∈𝒦∑r=1k∑ℓ∈[L]∖𝒞rBCE(𝟏[x^1ℓ=x1ℓ],qϕℓ(Tθ(x^r−1,k)))],x^1=argmax(Tθ(x^r−1,k))\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{ril-}\phi}(\phi):=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0},x_{1}}\bigg[\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}\sum_{r=1}^{k}\sum_{\ell\in[L]\setminus\mathcal{C}_{r}}\text{BCE}\left(\bm{1}[\hat{x}_{1}^{\ell}=x_{1}^{\ell}],\ q^{\ell}_{\phi}(T_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{r-1,k}))\right)\bigg],\quad\hat{x}_{1}=\arg\max(T_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{r-1,k})) (28)

with the argument of qϕq_{\phi} detached. The full objective is

ℒ⁡(θ,ϕ)=ℒtransport+λsemi​ℒsemi+λbnd​ℒbnd+λanchor​ℒanchor+λϕ​ℒϕ+λril​(ℒril-c+λquality​ℒril-​ϕ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi)=\mathcal{L}_{\text{transport}}+\lambda_{\text{semi}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{semi}}+\lambda_{\text{bnd}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{bnd}}+\lambda_{\text{anchor}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{anchor}}+\lambda_{\phi}\mathcal{L}_{\phi}+\lambda_{\text{ril}}\left(\mathcal{L}_{\text{ril-c}}+\lambda_{\text{quality}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{ril-}\phi}\right) (29)

The stop-gradient rollout costs kk extra forward passes and no extra backward pass during training. We implement qϕq_{\phi} as a head on the trunk of TθT_{\theta} reading its hidden state, so a refinement round costs exactly one NFE and the kk-round sampler requires only kk NFEs resulting in no inference overhead. An alternative instantiation for ril training is given in App. 12.

Self-Distillation with Semigroup Loss

Late in training, the output after kk refinement rounds approximates a clean sample from μ1\mu_{1}, and its coupling to the initial noise x0x_{0} is automatic, removing the need for a prescribed noise-data coupling. Writing x^r,k\hat{x}_{r,k} for the state after rr rounds under budget kk with x^0,k:=Tθ​(x0)\hat{x}_{0,k}:=T_{\theta}(x_{0}), the semigroup objective matches the map at every intermediate round to the final output:

ℒsemi-r​(θ):=𝔼x0,x1​[∑k∈𝒦∑r=1k∑ℓCE​(Tθ​(x^r−1,k),sg​(Tθ​(x^k−1,k)))]\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{semi-r}}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0},x_{1}}\bigg[\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}\sum_{r=1}^{k}\sum_{\ell}\text{CE}\left(T_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{r-1,k}),\text{sg}(T_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{k-1,k}))\right)\bigg] (30)

where x^k,k=Tθ​(x^k−1,k)\hat{x}_{k,k}=T_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{k-1,k}) is the final clean sequence after kk rounds of refinement. This is analogous to the semigroup loss defined in (18) but with the map operation composed with the renoise operation.

6 Experiments

We validate our claims empirically: (i) the autonomous flow on the simplex yields stable attractors at the vertices of the simplex, resulting in smoother trajectories; (ii) the timing of the phase transition is the optimal anchor time that prevents mode collapse and yields faster convergence; (iii) direct training of the one-step map scales to unconditional language modeling and reasoning benchmarks; and (iv) refinement-in-loop training improves coherence and accuracy.

6.1 The Autonomous Field Has Stable Attractors at the Vertices

In Figure 2, we compare the time-dependent flow matching field against the autonomous field on the 2-simplex: the autonomous field partitions the ambient space into basins where the only equilibria are the vertices, a property we analyze further for general simplices in App. 11.1. As illustrated in Figure 2E-G, the autonomous flow has straighter trajectories due to the stationary basins of attraction than the time-dependent flow, whose basins of attraction appear at staggered times in the interior of the simplex before moving to the vertices (App. 11.1.2).

6.2 Scaling the One-Step Map to Language

Experimental setup.

We evaluate unconditional generation on LM1B (Chelba et al., 2013) and OpenWebText (OWT) (Gokaslan et al., 2019), reporting generative perplexity (Gen-PPL) under GPT-2-Large (Radford et al., 2019) and within-sequence unigram entropy (Ent.). Since a model that collapses onto repeated tokens can reach arbitrarily low perplexity, we compare perplexities only among checkpoints whose entropy remains in the range of the data entropy. Baselines include distilled discrete diffusion and continuous flow map baselines evaluated at NFE budgets matched to ours. We report two variants: DBTM, trained with the transport, boundary, and anchor losses of Section 4.2, and DBTM + ril, which adds the refinement-in-loop objectives of Section 5.2. Further experiment details in App. 15.2.

Discrete BTM is competitive with distilled flow maps.

Table 1 compares against distilled few-step models and simplex flows at matched NFE. On LM1B, DBTM with ril outperforms every distilled discrete diffusion model at 1, 2, and 4 NFE, and is competitive with the best flow-map baseline while maintaining entropy close to the data. On OWT, with linear attention at matched parameter count, DBTM with ril achieves the lowest perplexity across all non-collapsed entropy methods at every NFE budget with the closest entropy to the data. At 4 NFE, DBTM without ril reaches the lowest perplexity overall (52.2) while DBTM + ril attains the highest entropy in the table (5.52), so the two variants trace the two ends of the quality-diversity frontier. Refinement-in-loop yields significant gains in the low NFE regime, reducing 1-NFE perplexity by 58% on LM1B and by 65% on OWT. Figures 1 and 3 show the resulting perplexity-entropy frontier, where DBTM and DBTM + ril dominate the baselines across entropies within the range of the data. Notably, DBTM requires no teacher flow, fewer training steps, and no time conditioning. Example generations are in App. 17.

Anchoring at the phase transition prevents mode collapse.

Theorem 4.1 gives t⋆t^{\star} as a function of the vocabulary size, noise scale, and schedule exponent. Sweeping tanchort_{\text{anchor}} around this value on LM1B (Table 12) demonstrates its importance. Anchoring before t⋆t^{\star} supervises toward a fixed target while the endpoint is undecided, and the model collapses to repetitive tokens, whereas anchoring after t⋆t^{\star} (e.g. tanchor=0.85t_{\text{anchor}}=0.85) leaves the post-transition interval unsupervised, resulting in higher Gen. PPL at equal training time (Table 12).

Refinement enables more effective use of step budget.

Table 7 evaluates a single DBTM checkpoint across NFE budgets: quality improves consistently with increasing budget until the sequence is fully committed, at which point it saturates. Distilled flow models instead move along a fixed time axis in discrete jumps, and masked diffusion unmasks on a fixed schedule with factorization error growing as NFE shrinks. Because every DBTM evaluation returns a clean-sequence distribution from any intermediate state, one model produces a one-shot proposal and then, via Section 5, renoises low-quality positions and remaps them against committed context. The commitment condition also acts as a self-stopping rule, so the NFE count adapts to the sample rather than being fixed in advance as in flow map and flow matching samplers.

6.3 Reasoning with Discrete BTMs

Experimental setup.

We evaluate on two conditional reasoning tasks, Sudoku at three difficulty levels, evaluated on one-shot exact-solve accuracy, and TinyGSM code (Liu et al., 2023a), evaluated on zero-shot accuracy on the GSM8K test set (Cobbe et al., 2021) following Kim et al. (2025). For baselines, we compare against many-step autoregressive, discrete diffusion, and continuous diffusion models as well as FMLM+ (Agarwal et al., 2026), a distilled few-step flow map model trained for iterative refinement. We match our NFE budget and network parameters to FMLM+ for fair comparison. Details in App. 15.

Refinement enables fixed-point reasoning.

Reasoning tasks are where the refinement scheme matters most, because a joint one-shot decode of a puzzle or a chain of arithmetic almost always contains locally plausible but globally inconsistent positions. Table 2 shows that DBTM matches or exceeds many-step autoregressive, discrete diffusion, and continuous flow baselines on all difficulty levels of Sudoku while using one to two orders of magnitude fewer network evaluations, and exceeds the strongest few-step baseline at the same budget, with the margin widening on the harder difficulty levels. On the 1319-problem GSM8K test set, DBTM achieves 0.8% solve accuracy in 1 NFE, surpassing continuous baselines CANDI (Pynadath et al., 2026) and FLM (Lee et al., 2026a) at 1024 NFEs and FMLM+ (Agarwal et al., 2026). At 32 NFEs, DBTM achieves 16.8% solve accuracy, slightly higher than FMLM+ at matched NFE and closing the gap with S-FLM at 32×\times fewer NFE. Autoregressive (AR) methods still dominate on GSM8K, suggesting refinement schemes that exploit the left-to-right structure of reasoning traces as a promising direction for future work.

7 Conclusion

We introduced Discrete Beckmann Transport Models (DBTM), a class of discrete generative models that replace the time-dependent velocity of flow matching with a stationary, autonomous field on the simplex. The resulting trajectories are straighter, time-averaged paths whose only stable equilibria lie at the vertices of the simplex. Defining the transport map as the solution to the conservation equation along this field lets us train it end-to-end from data alone, with no time conditioning and no teacher to distill from. Since every application of the map proposes a clean sequence, scaling NFEs take the form of renoise-and-refine steps that self-correct inconsistencies given a set of committed context tokens rather than finer integration steps. Across language modeling and reasoning benchmarks, DBTMs improve on both discrete diffusion and flow baselines.

9 Related Work

9.1 Discrete and Continuous Generative Models for Sequence Data

Generative modeling of discrete data in the form of sequences or graphs has taken many forms. Discrete diffusion (Austin et al., 2021; Lou et al., 2024), masked discrete diffusion (Shi et al., 2024; Sahoo et al., 2024; Ou et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025), and discrete flow matching (Gat et al., 2024; Campbell et al., 2024) model discrete sequence generation as a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) where transitions are defined by a rate matrix. However, since the discrete state space grows exponentially with the vocabulary size and sequence length, discrete diffusion models rely on learning the factorized approximations of the transition probabilities that require many inference steps to capture the dependencies between tokens for accurate generation (Kang et al., 2026). To overcome the factorization errors inherent in discrete state-space parameterizations, continuous state-space parameterizations have emerged as an alternative by embedding the flow trajectories in simplex space (Stark et al., 2024; Davis et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2025) or in a latent embedding space (Cheng et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026; Dieleman et al., 2022; Hu et al., 2026; Deschenaux and Gulcehre, 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Jo and Hwang, 2025). In this work, we model the autonomous flow transporting a Gaussian prior μ0\mu_{0} on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, d:=V​Ld:=VL, to the data distribution μ1\mu_{1} supported on the vertex set 𝒱:={e1,…,eV}L\mathcal{V}:=\{e_{1},\dots,e_{V}\}^{L} of the product of simplices (ΔV−1)L⊂ℝd(\Delta^{V-1})^{L}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, which is the construction used in discrete flow maps (Potaptchik et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026a).

9.2 Time-dependent and autonomous flows

Our framework develops the discrete state space instantiation of Beckmann Transport Models (BTMs) (Lee et al., 2026b), an approach to the problem of transporting states between distributions μ0\mu_{0} and μ1\mu_{1} via a time-independent velocity field bb that satisfies the divergence condition ∇⋅(ν​b)=μ0−μ1\nabla\cdot(\nu b)=\mu_{0}-\mu_{1}. In contrast to the time-dependent velocity field of standard flow matching (Lipman et al., 2023; Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2023; Albergo et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023b) that transports xx along bs​(x)=𝔼x0,x1​[I˙s|Is=x]b_{s}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0},x_{1}}[\dot{I}_{s}|I_{s}=x] which is the expectation of the interpolant velocity passing xx at time ss, the autonomous velocity field additionally averages over the time coordinate of the interpolant s∈[0,1]s\in[0,1], yielding the expectation over all interpolant velocities that pass xx at any time. In our work, we derive and empirically validate the unique properties of the autonomous flow on the simplex, specifically showing that it yields straighter flows with favorable Lipschitz properties and stationary attractors at the vertex. We establish the fact that the autonomous velocity field is non-vanishing approaching each vertex but vanishes when reaching it, partitioning the ambient space around the simplex into stationary basins of attraction.

9.3 Flow maps in discrete state space

There exists a long line of work on distilling and constructing few-step generative models that aim to reduce the number of function evaluations needed to integrate the generative ODE or SDE. These include consistency models (Song et al., 2023; Song and Dhariwal, 2024), shortcut models (Frans et al., 2025), MeanFlow (Guo et al., 2025), rectified flow (Liu et al., 2023b), flow maps (Boffi et al., 2024; Sabour et al., 2025; Boffi et al., 2025), and many of these frameworks have been extended to the discrete state space (Roos et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026a; Potaptchik et al., 2026) and variable-length generation (Tang and Chatterjee, 2026). Most related to our work are flow map language models (Lee et al., 2026a) with posterior refinement (Agarwal et al., 2026) and discrete flow maps (Potaptchik et al., 2026), which learn a two-time map (s,t)(s,t) along the interpolant between a Gaussian prior and the simplex vertices. Despite this shared goal, DBTM differs from flow maps in several aspects, summarized in Table 3.

Flow map models are explicitly time-conditioned and are typically trained by distilling a pretrained teacher flow btb_{t}, requiring supervision over all (s,t)(s,t) time pairs together with a careful balance of the diagonal (teacher matching) and off-diagonal consistency objectives. DBTM instead trains a single autonomous model conditioned only on the current state, with no teacher and no time embedding, reducing the space of functions that need to be learned during training. For a flow map, each NFE is a discretized jump along the generative trajectory, whereas for DBTM each NFE refines a complete clean proposal, so intermediate iterates remain in the data space and can be treated as a reasoning trace. Since inference only ever visits a small subset of the (s,t)(s,t) grid, flow map models spend training time on time pairs that are never used at sampling time. Training DBTM from noise-data interpolants instead covers exactly the states encountered at inference. Finally, the autonomous formulation admits a natural stopping criterion: sampling iterations stop once the proposal reaches its fixed point or once all tokens pass a confidence threshold, whereas flow map sampling requires the step schedule to be fixed in advance.

10.2 Divergence Condition

Proposition 10.1 (Autonomous flow satisfies divergence condition).

For uniformly sampled t∼𝒰⁡([0,1])t\sim\mathcal{U}([0,1]), the autonomous velocity b⁡(x):=𝔼t,x0,x1​[I˙t|It=x]b(x):=\mathbb{E}_{t,x_{0},x_{1}}[\dot{I}_{t}|I_{t}=x] satisfies the divergence condition:

∇⋅(b​ν)=μ0−μ1\displaystyle\nabla\cdot(b\nu)=\mu_{0}-\mu_{1} (31)

Proof. For a family of interpolants (αt,βt)t∈[0,1](\alpha_{t},\beta_{t})_{t\in[0,1]}, the time-dependent velocity, by the chain rule I˙t=α˙t​x0+β˙t​x1\dot{I}_{t}=\dot{\alpha}_{t}x_{0}+\dot{\beta}_{t}x_{1}, is:

bt​(x)=𝔼⁡[I˙t|It=x]=α˙t​𝔼​[x0|It=x]+β˙t​𝔼​[x1|It=x]=α˙t​η0​(t,x)+β˙t​η1​(t,x)\displaystyle b_{t}(x)=\mathbb{E}[\dot{I}_{t}|I_{t}=x]=\dot{\alpha}_{t}\mathbb{E}[x_{0}|I_{t}=x]+\dot{\beta}_{t}\mathbb{E}[x_{1}|I_{t}=x]=\dot{\alpha}_{t}\eta_{0}(t,x)+\dot{\beta}_{t}\eta_{1}(t,x) (32)

where we define η0​(t,x):=𝔼⁡[x0|It=x]\eta_{0}(t,x):=\mathbb{E}[x_{0}|I_{t}=x] and η1​(t,x):=𝔼⁡[x1|It=x]\eta_{1}(t,x):=\mathbb{E}[x_{1}|I_{t}=x]. btb_{t} satisfies the continuity equation with time-dependent marginal μt\mu_{t}:

∂tμt+∇⋅(bt​μt)=0\displaystyle\partial_{t}\mu_{t}+\nabla\cdot(b_{t}\mu_{t})=0 (33)

The autonomous flow is given by integrating over t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] of the time-dependent flow:

b⁡(x)=𝔼t​[bt​(x)|It=x]=∫01bt​(x)​μt​(x)​π​(t)​𝑑t∫01μt​(x)​π​(t)​𝑑t=1ν⁡(x)​∫01bt​(x)​μt​(x)​𝑑t\displaystyle b(x)=\mathbb{E}_{t}[b_{t}(x)|I_{t}=x]=\frac{\int_{0}^{1}b_{t}(x)\mu_{t}(x)\pi(t)dt}{\int_{0}^{1}\mu_{t}(x)\pi(t)dt}=\frac{1}{\nu(x)}\int_{0}^{1}b_{t}(x)\mu_{t}(x)dt (34)

where π⁡(t)\pi(t) is the distribution from which tt is sampled (typically uniform on [0,1][0,1]). For uniform π⁡(t)\pi(t), we can integrate the continuity equation over t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] to get:

∫01∂tμt​𝑑t+∇⋅∫01bt​μt​𝑑t=0,\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\partial_{t}\mu_{t}dt+\nabla\cdot\int_{0}^{1}b_{t}\mu_{t}dt=0, (35)

The first integral reduces to ∫01∂tμt​𝑑t=μ1−μ0\int_{0}^{1}\partial_{t}\mu_{t}dt=\mu_{1}-\mu_{0} and the second integral can be simplified using the definition of b⁡(x)b(x) in (34) to get (μ1−μ0)+∇⋅(b​ν)=0(\mu_{1}-\mu_{0})+\nabla\cdot(b\nu)=0 or ∇⋅(b​ν)=μ0−μ1\nabla\cdot(b\nu)=\mu_{0}-\mu_{1}. □\square

which is the first equality in (36). Since qxq_{x} integrates to one, Z⁡(x)<∞Z(x)<\infty and splitting the integrand linearly gives b⁡(x)=Z⁡(x)​η¯1​(t,x)−Z⁡(x)​x=Z⁡(x)​(η¯1​(t,x)−x)b(x)=Z(x)\bar{\eta}_{1}(t,x)-Z(x)x=Z(x)(\bar{\eta}_{1}(t,x)-x), which is the second equality. □\square

Remark 10.1 (Using the transport map to integrate the autonomous flow).

Since η1​(t,x)\eta_{1}(t,x) is a conditional expectation of x1∈M1x_{1}\in M_{1}, η¯1​(t,x)\bar{\eta}_{1}(t,x) is a convex combination of these and lies on the simplex η¯1​(t,x)∈(ΔV−1)L\bar{\eta}_{1}(t,x)\in(\Delta^{V-1})^{L} for every xx. Therefore, the autonomous velocity is fully determined by a map onto the product of simplices, which is exactly what Tθ:=softmax⁡(fθ)T_{\theta}:=\mathrm{softmax}(f_{\theta}) predicts. The trajectory of the autonomous flow is unchanged with respect to Z⁡(x)Z(x) up to a time reparameterization, so we only need to learn the map.

11 Theoretical Results

Here, we present the proofs and derivations for the theoretical results of our method. In App 11.1, we show the favorable properties of the time-dependent and autonomous flows, including the stationary attractors at the vertices. In App 11.2, we derive the commitment time of the stochastic interpolant to a vertex of the simplex as a function of the prior variance, the simplex dimension, and the exponent in the interpolant schedule. In App 11.3, we derive the form of the occupation measure defining the time spent at each point in ambient space. Finally, we show in App 11.4 that the autonomous flow velocity vanishes at the vertices.

11.1 Dynamics of Time-Dependent and Autonomous Flows

11.1.1 Autonomous Flow as Time-Averaged Dynamics

Proof.

Let u∼Unif⁡[0,1]u\sim\mathrm{Unif}[0,1] be independent of (x0,x1)(x_{0},x_{1}), so that (u,Iu)(u,I_{u}) has joint density (t,x)↦μt​(x)(t,x)\mapsto\mu_{t}(x) on [0,1]×ℝd[0,1]\times\mathbb{R}^{d}. Marginalizing in tt, the density of IuI_{u} is μ¯​(x):=∫01μs​(x)​𝑑s\bar{\mu}(x):=\int_{0}^{1}\mu_{s}(x)ds, and by Bayes’ rule the conditional density of uu given Iu=xI_{u}=x is μt​(x)/μ¯​(x)\mu_{t}(x)/\bar{\mu}(x) wherever μ¯​(x)>0\bar{\mu}(x)>0. By independence, 𝔼[I˙u∣u=t,Iu=x]=bt(x)\mathbb{E}[\dot{I}_{u}\mid u=t,\,I_{u}=x]=b_{t}(x), so the tower property gives:

b⁡(x):=𝔼u,x0,x1​[I˙u∣Iu=x]=𝔼⁡[bu​(x)|Iu=x]=∫01μt​(x)μ¯​(x)​bt​(x)​𝑑t\displaystyle b(x):=\mathbb{E}_{u,x_{0},x_{1}}[\dot{I}_{u}\mid I_{u}=x]=\mathbb{E}\big[\,b_{u}(x)\,\big|\,I_{u}=x\big]=\int_{0}^{1}\frac{\mu_{t}(x)}{\bar{\mu}(x)}b_{t}(x)dt (40)

which is (9). ∎

11.1.2 Attractors

Proposition 11.1 (Attractors of Autonomous Flow).

In the dynamical system

dd​t​Xs=b⁡(Xs),\frac{d}{dt}X_{s}=b(X_{s}), (41)

the only attractors are the vertices of simplex e1,…,eVe_{1},\dots,e_{V} at all time s∈[0,∞)s\in[0,\infty).

Proof.

The appendix 11.4 already proves that velocities vanish at the vertices e1,…,eVe_{1},\dots,e_{V}. By Proposition 3.1, given any initial point x0x_{0}, the trajectory XsX_{s} with Xs=0=x0X_{s=0}=x_{0} approaches one of the vertices as s→∞s\to\infty. Therefore, the basin of attraction of the vertices e1,…,eVe_{1},\dots,e_{V} partitions the space ℝV\mathbb{R}^{V}. Any additional attractor comes with a non-zero measure of basin of attraction, so there are no additional attractors. ∎

Now we study the dynamics of time-dependent flow matching

dd​t​Xt=bt​(Xt).\frac{d}{dt}X_{t}=b_{t}(X_{t}). (42)

We study the attractors of bt​(xt)b_{t}(x_{t}) for fixed time tt. As tt varies, the attractors of bt​(xt)b_{t}(x_{t}) move. The trajectory of (42) is pulled by attractors that move with time. We study bt​(Xt)b_{t}(X_{t}) making two assumptions below:

Assumption 11.1.
  1. (i)

    The prior is Gaussian x0∼𝒩⁡(c,σ2​𝑰V)x_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(c,\,\sigma^{2}\bm{I}_{V}) centered at c∈ℝVc\in\mathbb{R}^{V} with variance σ2\sigma^{2} and the prior is symmetric with ci=cjc_{i}=c_{j} for all ii and jj;

  2. (ii)

    The interpolant It=(1−t)​x0+t​x1I_{t}=(1-t)x_{0}+tx_{1} is linear.

Note that Assumption 11.1 (ii) is without loss of generality, because any straight line interpolant It=αt​x0+βt​x1I_{t}=\alpha_{t}x_{0}+\beta_{t}x_{1} is a time reparameterization of the linear interpolant It=(1−t)​x0+t​x1I_{t}=(1-t)x_{0}+tx_{1}. Our results hold for any linear interpolant up to a time reparameterization. The following lemma says that regardless of where the prior is centered, the attractors of bt​(xt)b_{t}(x_{t}) lie on the simplex ΔV−1\Delta^{V-1} for any tt.

Lemma 11.1 (Attractors Lie on Simplex).

For Gaussian prior x0∼𝒩⁡(c,σ2​𝐈V)x_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(c,\sigma^{2}\bm{I}_{V}) and any interpolant It=αt​x0+βt​x1I_{t}=\alpha_{t}x_{0}+\beta_{t}x_{1} and any time tt, all attractors lie on the simplex ΔV−1\Delta^{V-1}.

Proof.

We state without proof that the velocity bt​(xt)b_{t}(x_{t}) under Assumption 11.1 is

bt​(x)=11−t​(Dt​(x)−x),b_{t}(x)=\frac{1}{1-t}(D_{t}(x)-x), (43)

where the denoiser Dt​(x)D_{t}(x) takes the form

Dt​(x)=∑iwi​(x,t)​ei,withwi​(x,t)=softmaxi⁡(log⁡pi+t​xiσ2​(1−t)2−t​ciσ2​(1−t)),D_{t}(x)=\sum_{i}w_{i}(x,t)e_{i},\quad\text{with}\quad w_{i}(x,t)=\softmax_{i}\left(\log p_{i}+\frac{tx_{i}}{\sigma^{2}(1-t)^{2}}-\frac{tc_{i}}{\sigma^{2}(1-t)}\right), (44)

where cic_{i} is the ii-th coordinates of the center cc of the prior. For fixed tt, an attractor x=(xi)i=1,…,Vx=(x_{i})_{i=1,\dots,V} satisfies the equation bt​(x)=0b_{t}(x)=0, that is

xi=softmaxi⁡(log⁡pi+t​xiσ2​(1−t)2−t​ciσ2​(1−t)),x_{i}=\softmax_{i}\left(\log p_{i}+\frac{tx_{i}}{\sigma^{2}(1-t)^{2}}-\frac{tc_{i}}{\sigma^{2}(1-t)}\right), (45)

for i=1,…,Vi=1,\dots,V. Since x=(xi)x=(x_{i}) takes the form of a softmax, xx lie on the simplex ΔV−1\Delta^{V-1}. Notice that ci=cjc_{i}=c_{j} by Assumption 11.1 (i). The softmax equation (45) becomes cc-independent

xi=softmaxi⁡(log⁡pi+t​xiσ2​(1−t)2).x_{i}=\softmax_{i}\left(\log p_{i}+\frac{tx_{i}}{\sigma^{2}(1-t)^{2}}\right). (46)

∎

Lemma 11.2 (Asymptotic Formulae for Attractor Locations).
  1. (i)

    For small t≳0t\gtrsim 0, the coordinates of the unique attractor A∗A^{*} are

    xk=pk+pk​(pk−m2)σ2​t+𝒪⁡(t2),x_{k}=p_{k}+\frac{p_{k}\left(p_{k}-m_{2}\right)}{\sigma^{2}}t+\mathcal{O}(t^{2}), (47)

    for k=1,…,Vk=1,\dots,V, and m2=∑jpj2m_{2}=\sum_{j}p_{j}^{2} is the second moment of the target distribution.

  2. (ii)

    For large t≲1t\lesssim 1, there are VV attractors labeled by j=1,…,Vj=1,\dots,V. Let β=tσ2​(1−t)2\beta=\frac{t}{\sigma^{2}(1-t)^{2}}. The coordinates of the attractors AjA_{j} are respectively given by expansions in large β\beta

    xk=δk​j+ck​j​e−β+𝒪⁡(β​e−2​β),x_{k}=\delta_{kj}+c_{kj}\,e^{-\beta}+\mathcal{O}(\beta\,e^{-2\beta}), (48)

    for δk​j\delta_{kj} the Kronecker delta and the coefficients cj​kc_{jk} are given by

    ck​j={pkpj,k≠jpj−1pj,k=jc_{kj}=\begin{cases}\frac{p_{k}}{p_{j}},\quad&k\neq j\\ \frac{p_{j}-1}{p_{j}},\quad&k=j\end{cases} (49)
Proof.

(i) is shown by setting xk=pk+uk​t+𝒪⁡(t2)x_{k}=p_{k}+u_{k}\,t+\mathcal{O}(t^{2}) and plug into equation (45) to solve for coefficients uku_{k}.

For (ii), let u=1−tu=1-t and set xk=δj​k+rkx_{k}=\delta_{jk}+r_{k}. Taking the ratio of the kk-th and jj-th equation of (46) gives

xkxj=pkpj​exp⁡(t⁡(xk−xj)σ2​(1−t)2).\frac{x_{k}}{x_{j}}=\frac{p_{k}}{p_{j}}\exp\left(\frac{t(x_{k}-x_{j})}{\sigma^{2}(1-t)^{2}}\right). (50)

Since xj→1x_{j}\to 1 and xk→0x_{k}\to 0 for k≠jk\neq j as t→1t\to 1,

xk=pkpj​exp⁡(−tσ2​(1−t)2)​(1+o⁡(1)),k≠j.x_{k}=\frac{p_{k}}{p_{j}}\exp\left(-\frac{t}{\sigma^{2}(1-t)^{2}}\right)(1+o(1)),\qquad k\neq j. (51)

The expression for xjx_{j} then follows from ∑kxk=1\sum_{k}x_{k}=1. ∎

Remark 11.1.

The implication of Lemma 11.2 (i) is that, as tt increases from 00, the unique attractor A∗A^{*} moves towards the vertex ll with the largest target probability, pl=arg⁡maxk⁡pkp_{l}=\arg\max_{k}\,p_{k}. Since the first-order coefficient pk​(pk−m2)∼pk2p_{k}(p_{k}-m_{2})\sim p_{k}^{2} at k=lk=l is much larger than that at k≠lk\neq l. If a vertex kk has pk<pl2p_{k}<p_{l}^{2}, and hence pk−m2<0p_{k}-m_{2}<0, then the attractor will move away from vertex kk due to the negative first-order coefficient.

Lemma 11.2 (ii) establishes the existence of an attractor near each vertex at time t≲1t\lesssim 1. We are interested in when the attractor AjA_{j} associated with vertex jj appears. In Proposition 11.2, we show that the attractor AlA_{l} corresponding to the vertex with the largest target probability pl=arg⁡maxk⁡pkp_{l}=\arg\max_{k}\,p_{k} forms at t=0t=0. We call AlA_{l} the dominant attractor. Attractor AjA_{j} where j≠lj\neq l forms much later. In Proposition 11.3 and Corollary 11.1, we show that the time tjt_{j} at which attractor AjA_{j} forms is given in terms of the ratio between the target probability on the jj-th vertex and the highest target probability plp_{l}.

Proposition 11.2 (The Dominant Attractor).

The attractor AlA_{l} corresponding to the vertex with the largest target probability pl=arg⁡maxk⁡pkp_{l}=\arg\max_{k}p_{k} forms at time t=0t=0.

Proof.

We show that there is an attractor A∗A^{*} that exists for all time tt, and that attractor A∗A^{*} moves to vertex ll, the vertex with the largest target probability.

First, we notice that off-simplex directions are attracted to the vertex. The vector field bt​(x)b_{t}(x) restricting the simplex x∈ΔV−1x\in\Delta^{V-1} has the same attractors as the vector field x∈ℝVx\in\mathbb{R}^{V}. The off-simplex direction is the vector 𝟏\mathbf{1} of all 1s. Project the trajectory (42) onto 𝟏\mathbf{1}, we have

dd​t​⟨Xt,𝟏⟩=11−t​(⟨Dt​(Xt),𝟏⟩−⟨Xt,𝟏⟩).\frac{d}{dt}\langle X_{t},\mathbf{1}\rangle=\frac{1}{1-t}(\langle D_{t}(X_{t}),\mathbf{1}\rangle-\langle X_{t},\mathbf{1}\rangle). (52)

We rewrite scalar s=⟨Xt,𝟏⟩s=\langle X_{t},\mathbf{1}\rangle, and recall that ⟨Dt​(Xt),𝟏⟩=1\langle D_{t}(X_{t}),\mathbf{1}\rangle=1. The entries of Dt​(Xt)D_{t}(X_{t}) sum to 1 according to equation (44). Equation (52) becomes an equation of the projection ss

d​sd​t=1−s1−t.\frac{ds}{dt}=\frac{1-s}{1-t}. (53)

whose solution approaches s=1s=1 exponentially as tt increases. Since projections onto the off-simplex direction approach 1 exponentially, the off-simplex direction attracts. Hence the vector field bt​(x)b_{t}(x) restricting to the simplex x∈ΔV−1x\in\Delta^{V-1} has the same attractors as the unrestricted vector field for x∈ℝVx\in\mathbb{R}^{V}.

We focus on bt​(x)b_{t}(x) for xx on the simplex for fixed tt. Let x=(xi)i=1,…,Vx=(x_{i})_{i=1,\dots,V} and p=(pi)i=1,…,Vp=(p_{i})_{i=1,\dots,V} both be distributions. Let β1=tσ2​(1−t)2\beta_{1}=\frac{t}{\sigma^{2}(1-t)^{2}} and consider the potential function

V(x)=KL(x∥p)−β12∥x∥2.V(x)=\kl(x\,\|\,p)-\frac{\beta_{1}}{2}\|x\|^{2}. (54)

We show that V⁡(x)V(x) is a Lyapunov function. Denoting PiP_{i} as the ii-th softmax in (44) and ZZ is the shared denominator among PiP_{i} for i=1,…,Vi=1,\dots,V, the gradient of V⁡(x)V(x) against the ii coordinate is

The change of potential along bt​(x)b_{t}(x) is

bt​(x)⋅∇V​(x)\displaystyle b_{t}(x)\cdot\nabla V(x) =11−t​∑i(Pi−xi)​(−log⁡Pixi−log⁡Z+1)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{1-t}\sum_{i}(P_{i}-x_{i})(-\log\frac{P_{i}}{x_{i}}-\log Z+1)
=−11−t∑i(Pi−xi)logPixi,\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{1-t}\sum_{i}(P_{i}-x_{i})\log\frac{P_{i}}{x_{i}}, (56)

where we have moved the constants −log⁡Z+1-\log Z+1 out of the sum and applied ∑iPi=∑xi=1\sum_{i}P_{i}=\sum x_{i}=1. Rewriting the above equation, we have

bt(x)⋅∇V(x)=−11−t(KL(P∥x)+KL(x∥P))≤0,b_{t}(x)\cdot\nabla V(x)=-\frac{1}{1-t}(\kl(P\,\|\,x)+\kl(x\,\|\,P))\leq 0, (57)

where P=(Pi)i=1,…,VP=(P_{i})_{i=1,\dots,V}. The equality in (57) is obtained precisely when x=Px=P. That is, xx is an attractor as defined in equation (45). Let x∗x^{*} be the position of such an attractor. Define the Voronoi cell C={x|x∈ΔV−1,xl>xi, for all i≠l}C=\{x\,|\,x\in\Delta^{V-1},\ x_{l}>x_{i}\text{, for all $i\neq l$}\} as the set of points on the simplex whose closest point is the vertex ll. It is clear that the minimizer x∗x^{*} of V⁡(x)V(x) is in cell CC; otherwise, permuting the coordinates of x∗x^{*} yields a strictly lower value V⁡(x)V(x). Additionally, the minimizer of VV is unique by equation (55), where ∇iV​(x)=0\nabla_{i}V(x)=0 has a unique solution for generic values of pip_{i}.

We have shown there is a unique attractor A∗A^{*} corresponding to the minimum of V⁡(x)V(x), and A∗A^{*} is closest to the vertex ll. Now we show that as t→1t\to 1, the attractor A∗A^{*} approaches vertex ll. As t→1t\to 1, we have β1→∞\beta_{1}\to\infty, and the quadratic term in V⁡(x)V(x) dominates. Under the constraint ∑ixi=1\sum_{i}x_{i}=1, the quadratic term is minimized by x∗x^{*} with xj∗=1x^{*}_{j}=1 for some jj and xi∗=0x^{*}_{i}=0 for i≠ji\neq j. But since x∗∈Cx^{*}\in C, it must be the vertex ll with xl∗=1x^{*}_{l}=1. ∎

Proposition 11.3.

tj(1−tj)2≃σ2​β∗,where β∗−log⁡β∗=log⁡plpj+1+log⁡(m+1)\frac{t_{j}}{(1-t_{j})^{2}}\simeq\sigma^{2}\beta^{*},\quad\text{where }\ \ \beta^{*}-\log\beta^{*}=\log\frac{p_{l}}{p_{j}}+1+\log(m+1) (58)

for k≠ik\neq i. And the sum of the expressions (69) is infinity:

Note that Proposition 11.3 applies to both origin- and simplex-centered priors.

Corollary 11.1 (Attractors Form in Order).

Let plp_{l} be the largest target probability. For any j,k≠lj,k\neq l, if pj>pkp_{j}>p_{k}, then tj<tkt_{j}<t_{k}. That is, attractor AjA_{j} forms earlier than attractor AkA_{k}.

Proof.

For the right-hand side of (78), there are two choices of β1∗\beta^{*}_{1}, one greater than 1 and the other less than 1. We argue that we select the solution β1∗>1\beta_{1}^{*}>1. The Jacobian of the vector field bt​(x)b_{t}(x) in equation (43) is

where t⁡(β1)t(\beta_{1}) expresses tt in terms of β1=tσ2​(1−t)2\beta_{1}=\frac{t}{\sigma^{2}(1-t)^{2}}. The Jacobian is the xx-derivative of the map F⁡(x,β1)F(x,\beta_{1}). If at β1∗\beta_{1}^{*} and the attractor x⁡(β1∗)x(\beta_{1}^{*}), the determinant

detJ⁡(x)=detDx​F​(x,β1)≠0,\det J(x)=\det D_{x}F(x,\beta_{1})\neq 0, (84)

then by Inverse Function Theorem, there exists a neighbourhood BB around β1∗\beta_{1}^{*} and an neighbourhood UU around x∗x^{*} such that x⁡(β1):B→Ux(\beta_{1}):B\to U is a differentiable and satisfies

F⁡(x⁡(β1),β1)=0,F(x(\beta_{1}),\beta_{1})=0, (85)

for β1∈B\beta_{1}\in B. In other words, x⁡(β1)x(\beta_{1}) is a family of fixed points of bt⁡(β1)​(x)b_{t(\beta_{1})}(x). There is a lower time β1′=infB\beta^{\prime}_{1}=\inf B that is smaller than the threshold β1∗\beta_{1}^{*}, contradicting the assumption that β1∗\beta_{1}^{*} corresponds to the smallest time for attractor AjA_{j} to exist. Therefore detJ⁡(x)=0\det J(x)=0 at the threshold β1∗\beta_{1}^{*} for attractor AjA_{j}.

Write M=diag⁡x−x​x⊤M=\diag x-xx^{\top}, then according to equation (81), the matrix β1​M−I\beta_{1}M-I is singular at β1∗\beta_{1}^{*} and attractor x=x⁡(β1∗)x=x(\beta_{1}^{*}). Therefore, 1/β1∗1/\beta_{1}^{*} is an eigenvalue of the matrix MM. It is well-known that the largest eigenvalue of a matrix of the form MM is upper-bounded by maxi⁡xi\max_{i}x_{i}, and we have

1β1∗≤maxi⁡xi≤1.\frac{1}{\beta_{1}^{*}}\leq\max_{i}x_{i}\leq 1. (86)

We have shown that β1∗≥1\beta_{1}^{*}\geq 1. In this range, the mapping β1→β1−log⁡β1\beta_{1}\to\beta_{1}-\log\beta_{1} is increasing. In equation (58), a larger pjp_{j} corresponds to a smaller β1∗\beta_{1}^{*}, and thus a smaller appearance time tjt_{j}. ∎

Proposition 11.4 (Most Attractors Form Late).

Let the prior be standard Gaussian 𝒩⁡(c,𝕀)\mathcal{N}(c,\mathbb{I}) for cc subject to Assumption 11.1 (i). Except the dominant attractor AlA_{l}, no other attractors form earlier than t=12t=\frac{1}{2}.

Proof.

We show that tj≥12t_{j}\geq\frac{1}{2} for all j≠lj\neq l by a closer look at equation (86). The eigenvalue 1/β1∗1/\beta_{1}^{*} of M=diag⁡x−x​x⊤M=\diag x-xx^{\top} is smaller than the largest eigenvalue λmax\lambda_{\max} which we can write as

1β1∗≤λmax=max‖v‖=1⁡v⊤​M​v=max‖v‖=1⁡Varx⁡(v).\frac{1}{\beta_{1}^{*}}\leq\lambda_{\max}=\max_{\|v\|=1}v^{\top}Mv=\max_{\|v\|=1}\var_{x}(v). (87)

Where x∈ΔV−1x\in\Delta^{V-1} is a distribution and Varx⁡(v)\var_{x}(v) takes the variance of vv over xx. Let a=maxi⁡xia=\max_{i}x_{i}, b=mini⁡xib=\min_{i}x_{i} and c=(a+b)/2c=(a+b)/2 be the midpoint. By the bias-variance decomposition

𝔼x​[(v−c)2]=Varx⁡(v)+(𝔼x​[v]−c)2,\mathbb{E}_{x}[(v-c)^{2}]=\var_{x}(v)+(\mathbb{E}_{x}[v]-c)^{2}, (88)

and the variance is bounded by

Varx⁡(v)≤𝔼x​[(v−c)2]=∑ixi​(vi−c)2≤∑ixi​(a−b2)2≤a2+b22≤∥v∥22=12.\var_{x}(v)\leq\mathbb{E}_{x}\!\left[(v-c)^{2}\right]=\sum_{i}x_{i}(v_{i}-c)^{2}\leq\sum_{i}x_{i}\left(\frac{a-b}{2}\right)^{2}\leq\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}}{2}\leq\frac{\lVert v\rVert^{2}}{2}=\frac{1}{2}. (89)

Combining equation (89) and (87) gives β1∗≥2\beta_{1}^{*}\geq 2. When the prior has variance σ2=1\sigma^{2}=1, we have tj≥1/2t_{j}\geq 1/2. ∎

Proposition 11.3 and Corollary 11.1 show that for target distribution (pj)j=1,…,V(p_{j})_{j=1,\dots,V}, there are VV attractors, one corresponding to each vertex. The larger the probability pjp_{j} for vertex jj, the earlier the attractor AjA_{j} forms. From time t=0t=0 to 1, attractors form one by one in the interior of the simplex. By Proposition 11.2, the first formed attractor corresponds to the vertex/token of the highest probability pjp_{j}. Once an attractor AjA_{j} forms, it moves towards vertex jj according to Lemma 11.2 (i) and (ii). A trajectory that samples a low-probability vertex is pulled away at early times tt by the attractors that form earlier, which correspond to high-probability vertices/tokens.

Figure 4 illustrates this on a four-vertex example: the second attractor appears only after t=0.5t=0.5 despite its probability 0.380.38 being nearly equal to the dominant 0.40.4, so the dominant basin is the only one present for the first half of the flow. Figure 5 confirms the picture at scale: the predicted appearance times (58) match simulation up to V=100V=100 (Figure 5A), no non-dominant attractor forms before t=0.5t=0.5 in any simulation up to V=5000V=5000 (Figure 5B), and among non-dominant attractors, larger pjp_{j} form earlier (Figure 5C).

11.2 Deriving the Phase Transition and Commitment Time

Proof.

We want to determine the optimal tanchort_{\text{anchor}} for the anchor loss:

ℒanchor:=∑ℓ𝟏[t>tanchor]CE(T(It)ℓ,x1,ℓ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{anchor}}:=\sum_{\ell}\bm{1}[t>t_{\text{anchor}}]\text{CE}(T(I_{t})_{\ell},x_{1,\ell}) (100)

which preserves the diversity of generations. This means finding the smallest tanchort_{\text{anchor}} such that [tanchor,1][t_{\text{anchor}},1] is after the phase transition has occurred.

Bayes Posterior. Since the transport map is Tθ​(⋅)=softmax​(fθ​(⋅))T_{\theta}(\cdot)=\text{softmax}(f_{\theta}(\cdot)) acting on an intermediate state x=It∈ℝdx=I_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, independent of time, the minimizer of ℒanchor\mathcal{L}_{\text{anchor}} given xx is the Bayes posterior:

T⋆(x)=𝔼[x1|It=x,t≥tanchor]\displaystyle T^{\star}(x)=\mathbb{E}[x_{1}|I_{t}=x,t\geq t_{\text{anchor}}] (101)

This raises the question: for which tanchort_{\text{anchor}} is the interpolant at ItI_{t} committed to the target x1x_{1}? This can also be thought of as identifying the phase transition time in the autonomous flow.

Gibbs measure definition. Given x1=ekx_{1}=e_{k} and x0=z∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2​IV)x_{0}=z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I_{V}) with noise scale σ\sigma, the interpolant is given by:

x=It=(1−αt)ek+αtz,x|j=k∼𝒩((1−αt)ej,αt2σ2IV)\displaystyle x=I_{t}=(1-\alpha_{t})e_{k}+\alpha_{t}z,\quad x|j=k\sim\mathcal{N}((1-\alpha_{t})e_{j},\alpha_{t}^{2}\sigma^{2}I_{V}) (102)

By Bayes’ rule:

p⁡(j=k|x)\displaystyle p(j=k|x) =πj​p​(x|j=k)∑lπl​p​(x|j=l)\displaystyle=\frac{\pi_{j}p(x|j=k)}{\sum_{l}\pi_{l}p(x|j=l)} (103)
p⁡(x|j=k)\displaystyle p(x|j=k) =𝒩((1−αt)ej,αt2σ2IV)=(2πα2σ2)−V/2exp(−‖x−(1−α)​ej‖22​α2​σ2)\displaystyle=\mathcal{N}((1-\alpha_{t})e_{j},\alpha_{t}^{2}\sigma^{2}I_{V})=(2\pi\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2})^{-V/2}\exp\left(-\frac{\|x-(1-\alpha)e_{j}\|^{2}}{2\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2}}\right) (104)

Since (2πα2σ2)−V/2(2\pi\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2})^{-V/2} doesn’t depend on jj, it cancels in p⁡(j=k|x)p(j=k|x). Given ⟨x,ej⟩=xj\langle x,e_{j}\rangle=x_{j} and ‖ej‖2\|e_{j}\|^{2}, we can expand the squared distance as:

‖x−(1−α)​ej‖2=‖x‖2−2​(1−α)​xj+(1−α)2\displaystyle\|x-(1-\alpha)e_{j}\|^{2}=\|x\|^{2}-2(1-\alpha)x_{j}+(1-\alpha)^{2} (105)

The jj-independent terms cancel, and p⁡(x|j=k)p(x|j=k) reduces to:

p⁡(x|j=k)∝exp⁡((1−α)​xjα2​σ2)=:eβ⁡(t)​xj,β⁡(t):=1−αα2​σ2\displaystyle p(x|j=k)\propto\exp\left(\frac{(1-\alpha)x_{j}}{\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2}}\right)=:e^{\beta(t)x_{j}},\quad\beta(t):=\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2}} (106)

Substituting into the posterior gives:

p⁡(j=k|x)\displaystyle p(j=k|x) =πj​eβ⁡(t)​xj∑lπl​eβ⁡(t)​xl\displaystyle=\frac{\pi_{j}e^{\beta(t)x_{j}}}{\sum_{l}\pi_{l}e^{\beta(t)x_{l}}} (107)

which is the Gibbs or Boltzmann distribution over vocabulary VV at inverse temperature β⁡(t)\beta(t), tilted by the prior distribution π\pi, which we assume to be uniform πj=1/V\pi_{j}=1/V for simplicity. As t→1t\to 1 and α→0\alpha\to 0, we have β→∞\beta\to\infty and the posterior converges to the Dirac delta on the vertex p(⋅|x)→δkp(\cdot|x)\to\delta_{k}. As t→0t\to 0 and α→1\alpha\to 1, we have β→0\beta\to 0 and the posterior converges to the prior distribution p(⋅|x)→πp(\cdot|x)\to\pi.

Signal-to-Noise Ratio. The interpolant is split into a data component and a noise component:

It=(1−α)​ek⏟signal+α​z⏟noise,α=αt=(1−t)a,z∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2​IV)\displaystyle I_{t}=\underbrace{(1-\alpha)e_{k}}_{\text{signal}}+\underbrace{\alpha z}_{\text{noise}},\quad\alpha=\alpha_{t}=(1-t)^{a},z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I_{V}) (108)

where the signal is on the coordinate kk scaled with amplitude (1−α)(1-\alpha) and the noise spreads over all VV coordinates with standard deviation α​σ\alpha\sigma. So, the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) per coordinate is:

ρ:=ρ⁡(t)=signal amplitudenoise std=1−αα​σ\displaystyle\rho:=\rho(t)=\frac{\text{signal amplitude}}{\text{noise std}}=\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha\sigma} (109)

which can be interpreted as how much larger the signal is above the noise floor at time tt. For t→1t\to 1 near the data, ρ→∞\rho\to\infty and the target token is obvious, and for t→0t\to 0 near initial noise, ρ→0\rho\to 0 and the target is unknown. The SNR ρ\rho is monotonically increasing in tt, and σ\sigma and α\alpha determine how fast it increases.

Per-Particle Energies. Since (107) is a Boltzmann distribution, we can define the energy UjU_{j} for the vertex jj as:

Uj:=β(t)xj=β(t)(1−α)𝟏[j=k]+β(t)αzj\displaystyle U_{j}:=\beta(t)x_{j}=\beta(t)(1-\alpha)\bm{1}[j=k]+\beta(t)\alpha z_{j} (110)

With SNR ρ=(1−α)/α​σ\rho=(1-\alpha)/\alpha\sigma and β⁡(t)=(1−α)/α2​σ2\beta(t)=(1-\alpha)/\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2}, we can expand the energy as:

Uj\displaystyle U_{j} =(1−α)2α2​σ2𝟏[j=k]+1−αα​σ2zj\displaystyle=\frac{(1-\alpha)^{2}}{\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2}}\bm{1}[j=k]+\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha\sigma^{2}}z_{j}
=(1−αα​σ)2⏟=ρ2𝟏[j=k]+1−αα​σ2​zj⏟=:hj\displaystyle=\underbrace{\left(\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha\sigma}\right)^{2}}_{=\rho^{2}}\bm{1}[j=k]+\underbrace{\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha\sigma^{2}}z_{j}}_{=:h_{j}} (111)

Since zj∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2)z_{j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}), the variance of hjh_{j} is:

Var​(hj)=(1−αα​σ2)2​σ2=(1−αα​σ)2=ρ2\displaystyle\text{Var}(h_{j})=\left(\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha\sigma^{2}}\right)^{2}\sigma^{2}=\left(\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha\sigma}\right)^{2}=\rho^{2} (112)

So the energy of the posterior only depends on the SNR ρ\rho:

Uj\displaystyle U_{j} =ρ2𝟏[j=k]+hj,hj∼𝒩(0,ρ2)\displaystyle=\rho^{2}\bm{1}[j=k]+h_{j},\quad h_{j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\rho^{2}) (113)

Connection to Random Energy Model (REM). This has a nice connection with the Random Energy Model (REM) (Derrida, 1980) in statistical physics, which describes a system with MM states with i.i.d. random energies and partition function (normalization constant) Z=∑ie−βphys​ℰiZ=\sum_{i}e^{-\beta_{\text{phys}}\mathcal{E}_{i}}. The normalization of our posterior p⁡(j=k|x)p(j=k|x) is:

Z=∑j=1VeUj=eρ2+hk⏟target signal+∑j≠kehj⏟=:S\displaystyle Z=\sum_{j=1}^{V}e^{U_{j}}=\underbrace{e^{\rho^{2}+h_{k}}}_{\text{target signal}}+\underbrace{\sum_{j\neq k}e^{h_{j}}}_{=:S} (114)

where the sum of all non-target vertices SS is the REM partition function with M=V−1M=V-1 states, i.i.d. Gaussian energies hj∼𝒩⁡(0,ρ2)h_{j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\rho^{2}) at physical temperature βphys=1\beta_{\text{phys}}=1. Then, the probability of recovering j=kj=k from xx can be interpreted as whether the energy of state kk outweighs the competing energies j≠kj\neq k.

Phase Transition Point. Now, we want to find the point where the target energy dominates. For M=V−1M=V-1 states with i.i.d. 𝒩⁡(0,ρ2)\mathcal{N}(0,\rho^{2}) energies, we can count how many exceed a level h¯\bar{h}:

𝔼⁡[#⁡{j:hj≥h¯}]=M​Pr​(h1>h¯)≈M⁡(ρh¯​2​π​exp⁡(−h¯22​ρ2))≈exp⁡(log⁡M−h¯22​ρ2)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\#\{j:h_{j}\geq\bar{h}\}]=M\text{Pr}(h_{1}>\bar{h})\approx M\left(\frac{\rho}{\bar{h}\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(\frac{-\bar{h}^{2}}{2\rho^{2}}\right)\right)\approx\exp\left(\log M-\frac{\bar{h}^{2}}{2\rho^{2}}\right) (115)

The maximum non-target energy occurs when the expected count is equal to 1, i.e., log⁡M=h¯22​ρ2⟹h⋆=ρ​2​log⁡M\log M=\frac{\bar{h}^{2}}{2\rho^{2}}\implies h^{\star}=\rho\sqrt{2\log M}. Given M=V−1M=V-1, log⁡M≈log⁡V\log M\approx\log V and:

maxj⁡hj≈ρ​2​log⁡M≈ρ​2​log⁡V\displaystyle\max_{j}h_{j}\approx\rho\sqrt{2\log M}\approx\rho\sqrt{2\log V} (116)

Since the target coordinate has energy ρ2\rho^{2}, recovery of the target occurs when ρ2\rho^{2} surpasses the largest non-target energy ρ​2​log⁡V\rho\sqrt{2\log V}. The critical point is when ρ2=ρ​2​log⁡V\rho^{2}=\rho\sqrt{2\log V}, which for ρ>0\rho>0 yields:

ρ=2​log⁡V\displaystyle\rho=\sqrt{2\log V} (117)

We can define:

θ:=ρ2​log⁡V\displaystyle\theta:=\frac{\rho}{\sqrt{2\log V}} (118)

so that the critical point occurs when θ=1\theta=1.

Argmax Recovery. Taking the argmax coordinate k^=arg⁡maxj⁡p⁡(k=j|x)=arg⁡maxj​Uj\hat{k}=\arg\max_{j}p(k=j|x)=\arg\max_{j}U_{j} also leads to the critical point. The argmax coordinate is correct (i.e., k^=k\hat{k}=k) iff the energy of the target state kk dominates every non-target state:

Uk>maxj≠k⁡Uj⇔ρ2+hk>maxj≠k⁡hj\displaystyle U_{k}>\max_{j\neq k}U_{j}\iff\rho^{2}+h_{k}>\max_{j\neq k}h_{j} (119)

where hk∼𝒩⁡(0,ρ2)h_{k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\rho^{2}) is negligible given ρ2\rho^{2}. Then, we can count the number of non-targets that dominate the target as:

𝔼[#{j≠k:hj>ρ2}]≈Ve−ρ2/2=exp((1−θ2)logV)=V1−θ2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\#\{j\neq k:h_{j}>\rho^{2}\}]\approx Ve^{-\rho^{2}/2}=\exp((1-\theta^{2})\log V)=V^{1-\theta^{2}} (120)

which recovers the same critical point:

  1. (i)

    θ>1\theta>1: V1−θ2→0V^{1-\theta^{2}}\to 0 and none of the non-target states dominate the target, and the argmax is correct k^=k\hat{k}=k.

  2. (ii)

    θ<1\theta<1: V1−θ2→∞V^{1-\theta^{2}}\to\infty and many non-targets dominate the target and k^\hat{k} is a yields a random coordinate.

The critical point occurs when V1−θ2=1⇔θ=1V^{1-\theta^{2}}=1\iff\theta=1 and the target signal equals the maximum non-target ρ=2​log⁡V\rho=\sqrt{2\log V}.

Sharpness of Phase Transition. The maximum of VV Gaussians concentrates at maxj≠k⁡hj=ρ​2​log⁡V+𝒪⁡(ρ/log⁡V)\max_{j\neq k}h_{j}=\rho\sqrt{2\log V}+\mathcal{O}(\rho/\sqrt{\log V}) with Gumbel fluctuations. Writing ρ=2​log⁡V​(1+δ)\rho=\sqrt{2\log V}(1+\delta) and θ=1+δ\theta=1+\delta, the exponent becomes 1−θ2≈−2​δ1-\theta^{2}\approx-2\delta and the probability of error is approximately:

Pr​(error)≈V−2​δ=e−2​δ​log⁡V\displaystyle\text{Pr}(\text{error})\approx V^{-2\delta}=e^{-2\delta\log V} (121)

which is near 0 just above zero (i.e., δ>0\delta>0) and huge just below δ<0\delta<0. The phase transition occurs within the window when 2​δ​log⁡V=𝒪⁡(1)2\delta\log V=\mathcal{O}(1) of width δ=𝒪⁡(1/log⁡V)\delta=\mathcal{O}(1/\log V) which goes to zero as V→∞V\to\infty. Therefore, the probability curve sharpens to a step function as V→∞V\to\infty:

Pr(k^=k)→𝟏[ρ>2​log⁡V]asV→∞\displaystyle\text{Pr}(\hat{k}=k)\to\bm{1}[\rho>\sqrt{2\log V}]\quad\text{as}\quad V\to\infty (122)

Optimal tanchort_{\text{anchor}}. For αt=(1−t)a\alpha_{t}=(1-t)^{a}, the SNR is:

ρ⁡(t)=1−(1−t)a(1−t)a​σ\displaystyle\rho(t)=\frac{1-(1-t)^{a}}{(1-t)^{a}\sigma} (123)

is monotone in tt. Let t⋆t^{\star} denote the optimal tanchort_{\text{anchor}}, we can invert ρ⁡(t⋆)=2​log⁡V\rho(t^{\star})=\sqrt{2\log V} to get the optimal α⋆\alpha^{\star}:

2​log⁡V=1−α⋆α⋆​σ⟹α⋆=11+σ​2​log⁡V\displaystyle\sqrt{2\log V}=\frac{1-\alpha^{\star}}{\alpha^{\star}\sigma}\implies\alpha^{\star}=\frac{1}{1+\sigma\sqrt{2\log V}} (124)

and the optimal t⋆t^{\star}:

t⋆=1−(1+σ2​log⁡V)−1/a\displaystyle\boxed{t^{\star}=1-\left(1+\sigma\sqrt{2\log V}\right)^{-1/a}} (125)

which concludes the proof. ∎

11.2.1 Training Implications

Since the simplex dimension appears only in the logarithm 2​log⁡V\sqrt{2\log V}, when VV becomes large, large increases in VV result in small increases in t⋆t^{\star} (Figure 2D). The exponent on the interpolant schedule aa is inversely related to t⋆t^{\star} and moves the curve significantly for a∈{1,2,3}a\in\{1,2,3\} as shown in Figure 2D and H. Finally, increasing the scale σ\sigma of the prior Gaussian μ0=𝒩​(𝟎,σ2​𝑰V)⊗L\mu_{0}=\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I}_{V})^{\otimes L} results in a much larger increase in t⋆t^{\star}, since the initial point injects more uncertainty, resulting in a later commitment time. We show the impact of these parameters empirically in App 13.

11.3 Occupation Measure of Autonomous Flow on the Simplex

Proposition 11.6 (Explicit form of ν\nu and jj on simplex).

Let x0∼μ0x_{0}\sim\mu_{0}, with μ0\mu_{0} being a prior density on ℝV\mathbb{R}^{V} that decays exponentially towards infinity, and let x1∼μ1:=∑j=1Vpj​δejx_{1}\sim\mu_{1}:=\sum_{j=1}^{V}p_{j}\delta_{e_{j}} be independent of x0x_{0}, where {e1,…,eV}\{e_{1},\dots,e_{V}\} are the vertices of the simplex ΔV−1\Delta^{V-1}.
