Fix x∉{e1,…,eV}x\notin\{e_{1},\dots,e_{V}\} and let ϵj:=x−ej\epsilon_{j}:=x-e_{j}. We have the per-vertex occupancy ν(j)​(x)\nu^{(j)}(x) and current J(j)​(x)J^{(j)}(x) are given by:

ν(j)​(x)\displaystyle\nu^{(j)}(x) =pj​∫01αt−V​μ0​(ϵj+αt​ejαt)​𝑑t\displaystyle=p_{j}\int_{0}^{1}\alpha_{t}^{-V}\,\mu_{0}\left(\frac{\epsilon_{j}+\alpha_{t}e_{j}}{\alpha_{t}}\right)dt (126)
J(j)​(x)\displaystyle J^{(j)}(x) =pj​∫01αt−V−1​α˙t​ϵj​μ0​(ϵj+αt​ejαt)​𝑑t,\displaystyle=p_{j}\int_{0}^{1}\alpha_{t}^{-V-1}\dot{\alpha}_{t}\,\epsilon_{j}\,\mu_{0}\left(\frac{\epsilon_{j}+\alpha_{t}e_{j}}{\alpha_{t}}\right)dt, (127)

and for ν⁡(x)>0\nu(x)>0, the autonomous drift b=j/νb=j/\nu takes the form:

b⁡(x)=∑jJ(j)​(x)∑jν(j)​(x)\displaystyle b(x)=\frac{\sum_{j}J^{(j)}(x)}{\sum_{j}\nu^{(j)}(x)} (128)
Proof.

For categorical distributions on the simplex, we can write the target distribution as a weighted mixture of point masses μ1=∑jpj​δxj\mu_{1}=\sum_{j}p_{j}\delta_{x_{j}} where xj=ejx_{j}=e_{j} and e1,…,ede_{1},\dots,e_{d} are the dd vertices of the simplex Δd−1\Delta^{d-1}, each with probability pjp_{j}.

Rather than taking a ratio of measures, we define μt\mu_{t} and jtj_{t} weakly so that the per-vertex decomposition of the autonomous flow can be derived via expectations. For any test function φ∈C∞​(ℝV)\varphi\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{V}), we write:

∫φ⁡(x)​μt​(x)​𝑑x=𝔼⁡[φ⁡(It)],∫φ⁡(x)​jt​(x)​𝑑x=𝔼⁡[I˙t​φ​(It)]\displaystyle\int\varphi(x)\mu_{t}(x)dx=\mathbb{E}\left[\varphi(I_{t})\right],\qquad\int\varphi(x)j_{t}(x)dx=\mathbb{E}\left[\dot{I}_{t}\varphi(I_{t})\right] (129)

which is consistent with the definition bt=jt/μtb_{t}=j_{t}/\mu_{t} since taking the ratio or the right-hand identities yields 𝔼⁡[I˙t|It=x]​μt​(x)\mathbb{E}[\dot{I}_{t}|I_{t}=x]\mu_{t}(x) when tested against φ\varphi. Restricting x1=ejx_{1}=e_{j} gives us the per-vertex definitions of μt(j)\mu^{(j)}_{t} and Jt(j)J^{(j)}_{t} as:

∫φ(x)μt(j)(x)dx=𝔼[φ(It)𝟏{x1=ej}],∫φ(x)Jt(j)(x)dx=𝔼[I˙tφ(It)𝟏{x1=ej}]\displaystyle\int\varphi(x)\mu^{(j)}_{t}(x)dx=\mathbb{E}\left[\varphi(I_{t})\bm{1}_{\{x_{1}=e_{j}\}}\right],\qquad\int\varphi(x)J^{(j)}_{t}(x)dx=\mathbb{E}\left[\dot{I}_{t}\varphi(I_{t})\bm{1}_{\{x_{1}=e_{j}\}}\right] (130)

with the occupancy ν(j)​(x)=∫01μt(j)​(x)​𝑑t\nu^{(j)}(x)=\int_{0}^{1}\mu_{t}^{(j)}(x)dt and autonomous current J(j)​(x)=∫01jt(j)​(x)​𝑑tJ^{(j)}(x)=\int_{0}^{1}j_{t}^{(j)}(x)dt.

Step 1: Per-vertex occupancy. Since μ1\mu_{1} is a sum of point masses, ν\nu and jj can be decomposed for each vertex ν(j)\nu^{(j)} and J(j)J^{(j)}. Therefore, we can consider one atom first. If we fix atom jj, then x1=ejx_{1}=e_{j} and the only randomness in the interpolant is x0∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)x_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}). The interpolant at time tt is given by:

It=αt​x0+βt​ej\displaystyle I_{t}=\alpha_{t}x_{0}+\beta_{t}e_{j} (131)

Fixing It=xI_{t}=x, we can solve for x0​(x,t)x_{0}(x,t) to get:

x0​(x,t)=x−βt​ejαt=x−(1−αt)​ejαt=ϵj+αt​ejαt,\displaystyle x_{0}(x,t)=\frac{x-\beta_{t}e_{j}}{\alpha_{t}}=\frac{x-(1-\alpha_{t})e_{j}}{\alpha_{t}}=\frac{\epsilon_{j}+\alpha_{t}e_{j}}{\alpha_{t}}, (132)

where we have denoted ϵj=x−ej\epsilon_{j}=x-e_{j} and substituted βt=1−αt\beta_{t}=1-\alpha_{t}. Substituting into the Gaussian density of x0x_{0} gives a factor of:

Gt​(x)=μ0​(x0​(x,t))=μ0​(ϵj+αt​ejαt)\displaystyle G_{t}(x)=\mu_{0}\left(x_{0}(x,t)\right)=\mu_{0}\left(\frac{\epsilon_{j}+\alpha_{t}e_{j}}{\alpha_{t}}\right) (133)

Since the map x0​(x,t)↦It=αt​x0+βt​ejx_{0}(x,t)\mapsto I_{t}=\alpha_{t}x_{0}+\beta_{t}e_{j} is just a scaling of x0x_{0} by αt\alpha_{t} and a constant shift, its derivative is αt​Id\alpha_{t}I_{d}, and the density transforms via the inverse Jacobian αt−d\alpha_{t}^{-d}. Since the probability of selecting vertex jj is pjp_{j}, the pointwise density μt(j)​(x)\mu_{t}^{(j)}(x) at xx at time tt is:

μt(j)​(x)=pj​αt−V​Gt​(x)=pj​αt−V​μ0​(ϵj+αt​ejαt)\displaystyle\mu_{t}^{(j)}(x)=p_{j}\alpha_{t}^{-V}G_{t}(x)=p_{j}\,\alpha_{t}^{-V}\mu_{0}\left(\frac{\epsilon_{j}+\alpha_{t}\,e_{j}}{\alpha_{t}}\right) (134)

Then, the occupancy measure ν(j)​(x)\nu^{(j)}(x) is just μt(j)​(x)\mu_{t}^{(j)}(x) integrated over time t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] given by:

ν(j)​(x)=∫01μt(j)​(x)​𝑑t=pj​∫01αt−V​μ0​(ϵj+αt​ejαt)​𝑑t\displaystyle\nu^{(j)}(x)=\int_{0}^{1}\mu_{t}^{(j)}(x)dt=p_{j}\int_{0}^{1}\alpha_{t}^{-V}\mu_{0}\left(\frac{\epsilon_{j}+\alpha_{t}\,e_{j}}{\alpha_{t}}\right)dt (135)

Since αt→0\alpha_{t}\to 0 as t→1t\to 1, we have ϵj+αt​ejαt\frac{\epsilon_{j}+\alpha_{t}e_{j}}{\alpha_{t}} goes to infinity as t→1t\to 1. Hence the prior μ0​(ϵj+αt​ejαt)\mu_{0}(\frac{\epsilon_{j}+\alpha_{t}e_{j}}{\alpha_{t}}) decays exponentially as t→1t\to 1 offsetting the divergent αt−V\alpha_{t}^{-V}, and the integral in equation (135) is finite.

Step 2: Per-vertex current. Given x0​(x,t)=ejx_{0}(x,t)=e_{j}, the velocity I˙t\dot{I}_{t} is determined pointwise by xx since x0x_{0} is a function of ItI_{t} for all It=xI_{t}=x. Differentiating ItI_{t} and substituting x0=(ϵj+αt​ej)/αtx_{0}=(\epsilon_{j}+\alpha_{t}e_{j})/\alpha_{t}, we get:

I˙t=α˙t​x0+β˙t​ej=α˙tαt​(ϵj+αt​ej)+β˙t​ej=α˙tαt​ϵj\displaystyle\dot{I}_{t}=\dot{\alpha}_{t}x_{0}+\dot{\beta}_{t}e_{j}=\frac{\dot{\alpha}_{t}}{\alpha_{t}}(\epsilon_{j}+\alpha_{t}e_{j})+\dot{\beta}_{t}e_{j}=\frac{\dot{\alpha}_{t}}{\alpha_{t}}\,\epsilon_{j} (136)

where we have used α˙t+β˙t=0\dot{\alpha}_{t}+\dot{\beta}_{t}=0. Since j=b​ν=∫01bt​μt​𝑑tj=b\nu=\int_{0}^{1}b_{t}\mu_{t}dt, we:

J(j)​(x)=pj​∫01αt−V​(α˙tαt​ϵj)⏟I˙t​μ0​(ϵj+αt​ejαt)​𝑑t=pj​∫01αt−V−1​α˙t​ϵj​μ0​(ϵj+αt​ejαt)​𝑑t,\displaystyle J^{(j)}(x)=p_{j}\int_{0}^{1}\alpha_{t}^{-V}\underbrace{\left(\frac{\dot{\alpha}_{t}}{\alpha_{t}}\,\epsilon_{j}\right)}_{\dot{I}_{t}}\mu_{0}\left(\frac{\epsilon_{j}+\alpha_{t}\,e_{j}}{\alpha_{t}}\right)dt=p_{j}\int_{0}^{1}\alpha_{t}^{-V-1}\dot{\alpha}_{t}\,\epsilon_{j}\,\mu_{0}\left(\frac{\epsilon_{j}+\alpha_{t}e_{j}}{\alpha_{t}}\right)dt, (137)

by a similar argument to integral (135), the integral (137) is finite.

Step 3: Summing over vertices. Since μ1\mu_{1} is supported on {e1,…,eV}\{e_{1},\dots,e_{V}\} and the events {x1=ej}\{x_{1}=e_{j}\} partition the sample space such that ∑j𝟏{x1=ej}=1\sum_{j}\bm{1}_{\{x_{1}=e_{j}\}}=1 almost surely. For any test function φ\varphi, linearity of expectation gives:

∑j∫φ(x)Jt(j)(x)dx=∑j𝔼[I˙tφ(It)𝟏{x1=ej}]=𝔼[I˙tφ(It)∑j𝟏{x1=ej}]=𝔼[I˙tφ(It)]=∫φjtdx\displaystyle\sum_{j}\int\varphi(x)J^{(j)}_{t}(x)dx=\sum_{j}\mathbb{E}\left[\dot{I}_{t}\varphi(I_{t})\bm{1}_{\{x_{1}=e_{j}\}}\right]=\mathbb{E}\bigg[\dot{I}_{t}\varphi(I_{t})\sum_{j}\bm{1}_{\{x_{1}=e_{j}\}}\bigg]=\mathbb{E}\left[\dot{I}_{t}\varphi(I_{t})\right]=\int\varphi j_{t}dx (138)

and since this holds for all φ∈C∞​(ℝV)\varphi\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{V}), we can conclude jt​(x)=∑jjt(j)​(x)j_{t}(x)=\sum_{j}j_{t}^{(j)}(x)-a.e.. Analogously, μt=∑jμt(j)\mu_{t}=\sum_{j}\mu_{t}^{(j)} by the same argument with I˙t\dot{I}_{t} replaced by 11. Integrating over t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] and exchanging the sum and integral operations, we have:

ν⁡(x)=∫∑jμt(j)​(x)​𝑑t=∑jν(j)​(x),J⁡(x)=∫∑jJt(j)​(x)​𝑑t=∑jJ(j)​(x)\displaystyle\nu(x)=\int\sum_{j}\mu^{(j)}_{t}(x)dt=\sum_{j}\nu^{(j)}(x),\quad J(x)=\int\sum_{j}J^{(j)}_{t}(x)dt=\sum_{j}J^{(j)}(x) (139)

Since b=j/νb=j/\nu, we conclude:

b⁡(x)=∑jJ(j)​(x)∑jν(j)​(x)\displaystyle b(x)=\frac{\sum_{j}J^{(j)}(x)}{\sum_{j}\nu^{(j)}(x)} (140)

11.4 Autonomous Velocity Vanishes at the Vertices

Theorem 11.1 (Autonomous Velocity Vanishes at the Vertices).

Assume the interpolant αt∼(1−t)a\alpha_{t}\sim(1-t)^{a} as t→1t\to 1 with a≥1/Va\geq 1/V, and assuming the prior μ0​(x)\mu_{0}(x) tends to zero exponentially as x→∞x\to\infty, then at the vertices of the simplex, for all i=1,…,Vi=1,\dots,V, the autonomous velocity field b⁡(ei)=0b(e_{i})=0 when evaluated at vertices eie_{i}.

Proof.

For given eie_{i}, we evaluate J(j)​(ei)J^{(j)}(e_{i}) and ν(j)​(ei)\nu^{(j)}(e_{i}) for each jj. We compute ν(j)​(ei)\nu^{(j)}(e_{i}) and J(j)​(ei)J^{(j)}(e_{i}) for the case j=ij=i and j≠ij\neq i separately. First when j=ij=i, we have ϵi=ei−ei=0\epsilon_{i}=e_{i}-e_{i}=0 and

ν(i)​(ei)=pi​μ0​(ei)​∫01αt−V​𝑑t\displaystyle\nu^{(i)}(e_{i})=p_{i}\,\mu_{0}(e_{i})\int_{0}^{1}\alpha_{t}^{-V}\,dt (141)

For common choices of interpolant where αt∼(1−t)a\alpha_{t}\sim(1-t)^{a} as t→1t\to 1 with a≥1/Va\geq 1/V, the integral ∫01αt−V​𝑑t\int_{0}^{1}\alpha_{t}^{-V}\,dt diverges, and ν(i)​(ei)\nu^{(i)}(e_{i}) is positive infinity.

When j≠ij\neq i, we have ϵj=ei−ej=ei​j\epsilon_{j}=e_{i}-e_{j}=e_{ij} where ei​je_{ij} is the simplex edge between vertex ii and jj.

ν(j)​(ei)=pj​∫01αt−V​μ0​(ei​jαt+ej)​𝑑t\displaystyle\nu^{(j)}(e_{i})=p_{j}\int_{0}^{1}\alpha_{t}^{-V}\mu_{0}\left(\frac{e_{ij}}{\alpha_{t}}+e_{j}\right)dt (142)

As t→1t\to 1, we have αt→0\alpha_{t}\to 0. Assuming μ0​(x)\mu_{0}(x) tends to 0 exponentially fast as x→∞x\to\infty, the integral in (142) is finite. The denominator of b⁡(ei)b(e_{i}) is ν⁡(x)=∑jν(j)​(x)\nu(x)=\sum_{j}\nu^{(j)}(x). The denominator is infinite.

The numerator of b⁡(ei)b(e_{i}) is j⁡(ei)=∑J(j)​(ei)j(e_{i})=\sum J^{(j)}(e_{i}). Consider when the index j=ij=i. Since ϵi=0\epsilon_{i}=0, we have j(i)​(ei)=0j^{(i)}(e_{i})=0. When the index j≠ij\neq i, for the same reason as ν(j)​(ei)\nu^{(j)}(e_{i}), we have J(j)​(ei)J^{(j)}(e_{i}) is a finite number.

Overall, for all i=1,…,Vi=1,\dots,V, the autonomous velocity field b⁡(ei)b(e_{i}) is a ratio between a sum of finite vectors over positive infinity, and hence b⁡(ei)=0b(e_{i})=0. ∎

Proof. Notation. 12 Refinement-in-Loop Details and Additional Results

A core component of our training approach for DBTM is concentrating training time on states that are likely to be seen during inference, and therefore, minimizing the training-inference mismatch. To do this, we mimic the inference procedure of BTM, consisting of clean sequence proposals, renoising of low-quality tokens, and refining the proposal during training using the current model, and minimize the loss on these self-generated rollout states.

12.1 On-policy Rollouts

The standard method of constructing the context-dependent interpolant is to sample the fraction of clean tokens f∼𝒰⁡[0,1]f\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1] and apply an i.i.d. Bernoulli(ff) per position to determine whether it is in 𝒞\mathcal{C}. However, this creates a mismatch between training and inference since the context fed back into the model during refinement is not random. Instead, the context is largely dependent on how ’easy’ it is to be generated at the initial application of the transport map TθT_{\theta} and the subsequent refinement maps. To align the context seen during inference to the ones used for training, we apply an on-policy rollout step to generate a set of partial context sequences for training by running the same map, renoise, and refine steps as done during inference with a predetermined commitment condition.

Confidence-Based Selection

To determine which tokens to commit during the training-time rollouts, we use a confidence-based selection scheme. Given a coupling (x0,x1)(x_{0},x_{1}), for a rollout of depth kk, let x^r,k:=renoise​(Tθ​(x^r−1,k))\hat{x}_{r,k}:=\text{renoise}(T_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{r-1,k})) denote the state after rr refinement rounds without gradient tracking where x^0,k=x0\hat{x}_{0,k}=x_{0} is the initial noise state and x^k,k\hat{x}_{k,k} is the final clean sequence after kk rounds. After each round rr, we perform the following steps on the output of the previous round x^r−1,k\hat{x}_{r-1,k}:

  1. (i)

    Apply the parameterized transport map to get a clean proposal sequence Tθ​(x^r−1,k)T_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{r-1},k).

  2. (ii)

    Rank each position ℓ\ell by the model’s predicted confidence on the clean token value. Given the one-hot vector x1ℓx^{\ell}_{1}, compute the confidence at each position ℓ\ell as qℓ:=⟨Tθ​(x^r−1,k)ℓ,x1ℓ⟩q^{\ell}:=\langle T_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{r-1},k)^{\ell},x^{\ell}_{1}\rangle to get an ordered set ℛr\mathcal{R}_{r} of the uncommitted positions.

  3. (iii)

    Since there are kk total rounds, each round selects at minimum nr=⌈|ℛr|/(k−r+1)⌉n_{r}=\lceil|\mathcal{R}_{r}|/(k-r+1)\rceil highest confidence tokens to commit.

Since the map TθT_{\theta} is trained with the partial context interpolant, with more context yielding a sharper prediction task, this selection scheme uses the model’s own predictions to distinguish key structural tokens that are easy to predict without context from difficult, highly context-dependent tokens, and trains on the partial context sets it is likely to encounter during inference.

Committed vs. Non-Committed Clean Context

We perform two methods of refinement-in-loop training: either the clean context at each rollout step is committed or not committed. For the committed setting, at each iteration ii of the rollout with depth rr, we apply the current trained map Tθ​(x^i−1,r)T_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{i-1,r}), commit all tokens with qℓ≥κq^{\ell}\geq\kappa or at least nr=⌈|ℛr|/(k−r+1)⌉n_{r}=\lceil|\mathcal{R}_{r}|/(k-r+1)\rceil (defined as the set Δ​𝒞r\Delta\mathcal{C}_{r}) where ℛr\mathcal{R}_{r} are the uncommitted tokens, and reset the remaining tokens back to their coupled noise state x0ℓx_{0}^{\ell} for ℓ∈[L]∖𝒞r\ell\in[L]\setminus\mathcal{C}_{r}. After the rollout step, the loss in (27) is computed on only the uncommitted tokens [L]∖𝒞r[L]\setminus\mathcal{C}_{r} at each rollout depth rr:

ℒril-c​(θ):=𝔼x0,x1​[∑k∈𝒦∑r=1k∑ℓ∈[L]∖𝒞rCE​(Tθ​(x^r−1,k)ℓ,x1ℓ)]\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{ril-c}}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0},x_{1}}\bigg[\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}\sum_{r=1}^{k}\sum_{\ell\in[L]\setminus\mathcal{C}_{r}}\text{CE}\left(T_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{r-1,k})^{\ell},x_{1}^{\ell}\right)\bigg] (166)

where ril-c denotes the loss for the committing rollout setting. We can also define the transport loss (17) and anchor loss (21) on these refinement-generated context sets, with ℓ∈[L]∖𝒞r\ell\in[L]\setminus\mathcal{C}_{r} being the uncommitted tokens that the loss is computed over.

For the non-committed setting, at each iteration ii of the rollout with depth rr, we apply the current trained map Tθ​(x^i−1,r)T_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{i-1,r}), but instead hold the highest confidence tokens in set 𝒞r\mathcal{C}_{r}, such that they remain in their mapped categorical state x^i,rℓ←Tθ​(x^i−1,r)ℓ∈ΔV−1\hat{x}^{\ell}_{i,r}\leftarrow T_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{i-1,r})^{\ell}\in\Delta^{V-1} for ℓ∈𝒞r\ell\in\mathcal{C}_{r} and can be changed in the next round of refinement. The remaining tokens are similarly reset to their coupled noise state x^i,rℓ←x0ℓ\hat{x}^{\ell}_{i,r}\leftarrow x_{0}^{\ell} for ℓ∈[L]∖𝒞r\ell\in[L]\setminus\mathcal{C}_{r}. After rollout, the loss is now computed on all the tokens in the map output at each rollout depth rr:

ℒril-nc​(θ):=𝔼x0,x1​[∑k∈𝒦∑r=1k∑ℓ∈[L]CE​(Tθ​(x^r−1,k)ℓ,x1ℓ)]\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{ril-nc}}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0},x_{1}}\bigg[\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}\sum_{r=1}^{k}\sum_{\ell\in[L]}\text{CE}\left(T_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{r-1,k})^{\ell},x_{1}^{\ell}\right)\bigg] (167)

where the sum is taken over all token positions ℓ∈[L]\ell\in[L] instead of only the uncommitted set and ril-nc denotes the loss for the non-committed rollout setting.

Matching Deeper Rollouts with Self-Distillation

Since the noise-data coupling is generally not well-defined for unconditional text generation where there is no prompt and the space of possible clean outputs is large, supervising intermediate rollouts only with clean data samples can prevent the model from generating diverse text since it forces intermediate states to produce a single output even when that output is not aligned with its generative trajectory.

Therefore, to encourage coherent yet diverse supervision, we incorporate a form of self-distillation into the objective. After a warm-up stage where the model starts to generate coherent text for some k∈𝒦k\in\mathcal{K}, we can use the categorical outputs of the map after the kkth round Tθ​(x^k−1,k)∈(ΔV−1)LT_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{k-1,k})\in(\Delta^{V-1})^{L} as the target to which the map applied to earlier refinement rounds r<kr<k is supervised:

ℒsoft-ril-c​(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{soft-ril-c}}(\theta) :=𝔼x0,x1​[∑k∈𝒦∑r=1k∑ℓ∈[L]∖𝒞rCE​(Tθ​(x^r−1,k)ℓ,sg​(Tθ​(x^k−1,k)ℓ))]\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0},x_{1}}\bigg[\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}\sum_{r=1}^{k}\sum_{\ell\in[L]\setminus\mathcal{C}_{r}}\text{CE}\left(T_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{r-1,k})^{\ell},\text{sg}(T_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{k-1,k})^{\ell})\right)\bigg] (168)
ℒsoft-ril-nc​(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{soft-ril-nc}}(\theta) :=𝔼x0,x1​[∑k∈𝒦∑r=1k∑ℓ∈[L]CE​(Tθ​(x^r−1,k)ℓ,sg​(Tθ​(x^k−1,k)ℓ))]\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0},x_{1}}\bigg[\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}\sum_{r=1}^{k}\sum_{\ell\in[L]}\text{CE}\left(T_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{r-1,k})^{\ell},\text{sg}(T_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{k-1,k})^{\ell})\right)\bigg] (169)

where soft denotes that the target can be any categorical distribution on the interior of the simplex rather than only one-hot vectors on the vertices.

12.2 Refinement-in-Loop for Reasoning

Setup

In the Sudoku setting, the prior state x0x_{0} is not just Gaussian noise but a 9×99\times 9 grid with a set of filled-in numbers as clues depending on the difficulty (easy: 40, medium: 35, hard: 30), which each correspond exactly to one solution x1x_{1}. Therefore, given x0x_{0}, there is no uncertainty about what the answer x1x_{1} should be, so x1x_{1} should be the only supervision target, and self-distillation is unnecessary, since the self-generated supervision target can only be either equivalent to x1x_{1} or incorrect.

Instead, we test the effect of refinement-in-loop only with the defined (x0,x1)(x_{0},x_{1}) data couplings and no self-distillation. We set the maximum depth to k=4k=4 NFEs (initial map + three refinement rounds), and for each round r∈{1,…,k}r\in\{1,\dots,k\} perform refinement by committing the positions with the highest ground-truth confidence, reset the uncommitted positions to their prior state x0ℓx_{0}^{\ell} for ℓ∈[L]∖𝒞r\ell\in[L]\setminus\mathcal{C}_{r} to form a set of self-rollout states x^r,k\hat{x}_{r,k} for supervising against the ground truth via the ril-c loss in (166). A summary of experiment settings is provided in Table 5.

Results

In Table 2, we show that DBTM with refinement-in-loop (DBTM + ril) achieves superior performance against all baselines and difficulty levels with only 4 NFEs, 32×32\times fewer NFEs than autoregressive, discrete diffusion, and continuous diffusion baselines, and matched NFEs with the closest flow map language model baseline, FMLM+ (Agarwal et al., 2026). Notably, on Sudoku Hard, DBTM + ril surpasses FMLM+ by 16.1%16.1\% at 16 NFEs and 13.4%13.4\% at 4 NFEs. As shown in Figure 6, DBTM trained on the clean-context interpolant can converge to high solve accuracy without ril training, but DBTM + ril significantly accelerates convergence while achieving higher accuracy.

12.3 Refinement-in-Loop for Unconditional Language Modeling

Setup

In the language modeling task, there is no definitive coupling between noise and data, since, given a noise sample x0x_{0}, any coherent text sequence is a valid target sample x1x_{1} and there is no ’right’ or ’wrong’ answer like in the reasoning case. Defining a random coupling between noise and data and supervising the on-policy rollouts from the noise to match the data is susceptible to mode collapse, since the noise can be close to generating a completely different, but still coherent, sequence before it is forced to match an arbitrary target. This differs from the base training procedure where the intermediate states are constructed from the interpolant defined as a function of both x0x_{0} and x1x_{1}.

We avoid mode collapse in two complementary ways. First, we use minibatch optimal transport (Tong et al., 2024) to define the coupling (x0,x1)(x_{0},x_{1}) for supervised ril training and test both the committed and non-committed clean context methods described in App 12.1 with either the target x1x_{1} being committed or held at the categorical state at the positions where the map is most confident. Second, we perform self-distillation after a warmup phase in parallel to the data-supervised training as described in App 12.1, where the target is a function of the noise input x0x_{0}, making the self-generated and refined sequence a well-defined target. We use the LM1B dataset as a testbed for these methods and provide a summary of experiment settings in Table 5.

Results

In Figure 3 and Table 13, we show that DBTM with refinement-in-loop (commit) achieves the widest Pareto frontier of all methods, with low Gen. PPL across all entropy values from 3.90−4.303.90-4.30. Notably, DBTM + ril achieves the lowest PPL along the frontier curve across all NFE counts and methods. When comparing commit vs. non-commit ril training, we found that the commit mode consistently achieves lower Gen. PPL across NFE counts and selection thresholds with stable entropy around 4.004.00 (Table 6). Figure 7 plots the Gen. PPL and sample entropy from small validation batches over training steps. Visually, Gen. PPL rises early in training as entropy approaches the data entropy, and when on-policy training turns on after the 100​K100\mathrm{K}- step warmup, Gen. PPL starts to drop while entropy remains stable. In Figure 7A-C, the commit method (purple curve) shows a steeper drop in Gen. PPL than the non-commit method (turquoise curve).

13 Hyperparameter Discussion

Below, we discuss each ablated hyperparameter, what it controls, and the behavior that the sweeps in Table 10 show. App 13.1 describes the training-time knobs of the map, and App 13.2 describes the inference-time knobs that can be changed on a fixed checkpoint.

13.1 Training Hyperparameters

Adaptive Loss

To stabilize training, we scale the losses with a gradient-detached weight that downweights large mismatches in the predicted and true target. Denoting the transport map prediction q⁡(x)=T⁡(x)∈ΔV−1q(x)=T(x)\in\Delta^{V-1} and p⁡(x)=sg​(T⁡(x)+I˙t​(x)⋅∇T​(x))p(x)=\texttt{sg}(T(x)+\dot{I}_{t}(x)\cdot\nabla T(x)), we write the mismatch as Δ⁡(x)=q⁡(x)−p⁡(x)\Delta(x)=q(x)-p(x) and the weight as:

w⁡(x):=sg​[(‖Δ⁡(x)‖22+c)−r]\displaystyle w(x):=\texttt{sg}\left[\left(\|\Delta(x)\|^{2}_{2}+c\right)^{-r}\right] (170)

where cc and rr are tunable hyperparameters.

Minimum Anchor Time

The threshold tanchort_{\text{anchor}} gates the anchor loss, which supervises Tθ​(It)T_{\theta}(I_{t}) directly toward x1x_{1} only for t>tanchort>t_{\text{anchor}} and sets how much of the interpolant is treated as already committed. We prove in App. 11.2 that the optimal anchor time aligns closely with the time of the phase transition and perform an ablation over tanchort_{\text{anchor}} on LM1B in Table 12.

Noise Scale

The prior scale σ\sigma in μ0=𝒩​(0,σ2​𝑰V)⊗L\mu_{0}=\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}\bm{I}_{V})^{\otimes L} sets the radius of the Gaussian hypersphere around the simplex, and enters the commitment time through the signal-to-noise ratio ρ⁡(t)=(1−αt)/αt​σ\rho(t)=(1-\alpha_{t})/\alpha_{t}\sigma (See App 11.2 and Figure 2). Raising it to σ=1.2\sigma{=}1.2 improves Gen-PPL at every NFE budget (178.1 vs. 247.1 at NFE 1, 61.9 vs. 70.1 at NFE 8) but drops entropy below 4 (Table 10).

Schedule Exponent

The exponent aa in αt=(1−t)a\alpha_{t}=(1-t)^{a} controls how quickly the interpolant resolves onto a vertex, and for larger aa, this reduces the commitment time t⋆t^{\star} (Figure 2). Setting a=1a{=}1 reduces to the linear interpolant It=(1−t)​x0+t​x1I_{t}=(1-t)x_{0}+tx_{1}.

Adaptive Loss Constant

The constant cc in the adaptive weight w⁡(x)=sg​[(‖Δ⁡(x)‖22+c)−r]w(x)=\texttt{sg}[(\|\Delta(x)\|_{2}^{2}+c)^{-r}] determines how strongly a large prediction mismatch is downweighted, with small cc giving a more aggressive reweighting. It is the least sensitive knob we swept, where moving cc from 11 to 10−510^{-5} changes Gen-PPL negligibly and leaves entropy unchanged, demonstrating that our method is robust to minor tuning in the objective.

13.2 Inference Hyperparameters

Rounds of Refinement

Each round is one map application and one NFE with no additional NFE from computing the confidence or quality score, so the number of rounds KK is equivalent to the number of jumps taken with a flow map or integration steps taken with a flow matching model. Quality improves consistently with increasing kk until the sampler saturates when every position is committed to a token.

Commit Scorer

The scorer ranking positions for commitment is either the map’s own softmax confidence (rounding error of argmax token) or the learned per-token quality qϕq_{\phi}. All positions with score larger than the confidence threshold κ\kappa are committed. The sampler commits a minimum of nr=⌈|ℛr|/(k−r+1)⌉n_{r}=\lceil|\mathcal{R}_{r}|/(k-r+1)\rceil highest-scoring uncommitted positions at round regardless of whether their score exceeds κ\kappa, which guarantees the sampler finishes within its NFE budget.

Confidence Threshold

The threshold κ\kappa decides which positions are committed rather than renoised, with position ℓ\ell frozen when qℓ≥κq^{\ell}\geq\kappa. Its effect depends on whether the per-round minimum commit count nr=⌈|ℛr|/(k−r+1)⌉n_{r}=\lceil|\mathcal{R}_{r}|/(k-r+1)\rceil is met.

Commit Temperature

Temperature used to scale the proposed categorical probabilities before taking the softmax Tθ​(x0):=softmax​(fθ​(x0)/temp)T_{\theta}(x_{0}):=\text{softmax}(f_{\theta}(x_{0})/\texttt{temp}). When temp=0.0\texttt{temp}=0.0, the committed token is the argmax.

Prior Scale

The standard deviation σ\sigma of the Gaussian prior distribution from which the initial noise latent at each position ℓ\ell are sampled x0ℓ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,σ2​𝑰V)x^{\ell}_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\sigma^{2}\bm{I}_{V}).

Repetition Penalty

For unconditional language modeling, the commit rule reads each position’s marginal independently within a round can cause repetition between tokens committed within a single round. As is standard for autoregressive decoding (Keskar et al., 2019), we apply a repetition penalty λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 that divides Tθ​(x)jℓT_{\theta}(x)^{\ell}_{j} by (1+nj​(𝒞))λ(1+n_{j}(\mathcal{C}))^{\lambda} on uncommitted tokens before decoding and scoring, where nj​(𝒞)n_{j}(\mathcal{C}) counts committed positions holding token jj, which has no effect for 1 NFE sampling. We find that after refinement-in-loop training, the penalty is not required for coherent sampling, demonstrating that training on contexts seen during inference improves generation quality.

Integrating the Autonomous Flow

We empirically determine the hitting time on LM1B by integrating the time-independent velocity implied by the trained map over a range of horizons HH (Table 9). At short horizons (H=1H=1), the integrated trajectory does not reach the correct basin of attraction, but by the time the horizon increases to H=4H=4, the integrated field has settled onto a fixed point x∈M1x\in M_{1} where b⁡(x)=0b(x)=0, and sample quality no longer improves as the horizon grows to H=8H=8. However, we empirically observe that applying the one-step map Tθ​(x)T_{\theta}(x) consistently outperforms integrating the implied velocity field, even with fine discretization steps (Nsteps=64N_{\text{steps}}=64). This supports scaling refinements of the one-step map rather than scaling integration steps, and is the property that motivates the refinement scheme of Section 5.

15 Experiment Details

15.1 General Experiment Details

Training Details

All models use AdamW (β1=0.9\beta_{1}{=}0.9, β2=0.999\beta_{2}{=}0.999, ϵ=10−8\epsilon{=}10^{-8}) in bf16, zero weight decay, gradient clipping at 1.01.0, and peak learning rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} with linear warmup. We maintain an exponential moving average (EMA) of the map weights with decay 0.99990.9999, and a second, independent EMA of the predictor ϕ\phi with the same decay. All reported results use the EMA weights. The global batch is given by per-GPU batch ×\times devices ×\times accumulation, so runs reproduce at any device count: 512512 (per-GPU 128128) for language modeling, 256256 for reasoning.

Architecture

The backbone architecture is a DiT (Peebles and Xie, 2023) with adaLN conditioning (dimension 128128) and rotary positional embeddings (Su et al., 2024), acting on a continuous (B,L,V)(B,L,V) simplex latent without conditioning on time tt. Language modeling and TinyGSM use 768768 hidden / 1212 layers / 1212 heads, Sudoku 512512 / 88 / 88, all with FFN multiplier 44, dropout 0.10.1, untied embeddings, and a tanh\tanh softcap of 5050 on attention logits (Table 15).

Fused Kernel for JVP Computation

The transport loss (17) is defined through I˙t⋅∇Tθ​(It)\dot{I}_{t}\cdot\nabla T_{\theta}(I_{t}), so each step needs a Jacobian-vector product (JVP) through the network, evaluated in forward mode. This dominates our training cost since it requires materializing the (B, heads, L, L) score tensor. We instead use a fused Triton kernel (Zhou et al., 2026) that computes the attention output and its derivative together in a single streaming pass, so the full score tensor is never held in memory. The two passes share one sweep over the keys and values: the ordinary forward pass only reserves the output buffers, and the kernel fills them while computing the derivative.

Backpropagation is handled by two separate kernels, one for the output and the derivative, which can be cleanly switched off to the standard JVP mechanism by setting fast_jvp_attn=false. Measured on an A100 over a four-block DiT, it cuts peak memory by 1.4×1.4\times at B=64B{=}64, L=128L{=}128, V=12V{=}12 and by 3.7×3.7\times at B=8B{=}8, L=1024L{=}1024, V=8192V{=}8192, with a 1.2×1.2\times and 1.7×1.7\times speedup respectively, while matching the unfused implementation to a cosine similarity of at least 0.999990.99999 on the prediction, the derivative, and the gradients. One limitation is that the kernel does not implement the tanh\tanh softcap on attention logits. We therefore checked on each task that the logits stay well below the cap before using the fused kernel.

15.2 Unconditional Language Modeling Experiment Details

Datasets and Tokenization

LM1B uses the bert-base-uncased tokenizer (V=30,522V{=}30{,}522) at length 128128 and OpenWebText uses GPT-2 BPE (V=50,257V{=}50{,}257) at length 10241024. Documents are concatenated and wrapped into fixed-length blocks with EOS at every boundary, so all sequences are full and no padding is needed.

Linear-Attention Backbone

The DBTM + lin rows replace nine of the twelve attention blocks with bidirectional gated delta-rule mixers following DeltaFlow (Guo et al., 2026), keeping full attention at every fourth block ([gdn,gdn,gdn,attn], chunk size 256, alternating scan direction). Each gated DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024) runs forward and backward over the sequence. Since DBTM is autonomous, the decay and write-rate gates that DeltaFlow conditions on diffusion time are instead conditioned on the current simplex state. We do not use DeltaFlow’s temporal-state-consistency loss. Hidden size, depth, heads, dropout, the predictor ϕ\phi and every training knob are identical to the DiT architecture with matched parameter count (171.9M for attention, 177.5M for linear), so the two backbones differ only in the attention mechanism. The linear rows are trained from scratch at the same batch size and learning rate and reported at the same step count. The delta-rule attention mechanism costs time linear in the sequence length LL, whereas dense attention costs quadratic. In Figure 1, Table 1, and Table 7, we show the linear architecture on OpenWebText (L=1024L{=}1024) as a proof-of-concept for long-context modeling.

Training Configuration

Both datasets use a global batch of 512512 and 10,00010{,}000 warmup steps, a linear interpolant with σ=1.0\sigma{=}1.0, tanchor=0.75t_{\text{anchor}}{=}0.75, OT coupling, uniform time sampling, adaptive transport and cross-entropy endpoint losses, and the clean_context per-token schedule, which trains the map on partially committed sequences and so matches the refinement sampler.

Baselines

For unconditional language modeling on LM1B and OWT, we compare DBTM against distilled discrete diffusion methods, including Duo (Sahoo et al., 2025) with DCD (Sahoo et al., 2025), MDLM (Sahoo et al., 2024) with SDTT (Deschenaux and Gulcehre, 2025), and both Duo and MDLM with Di4C (Hayakawa et al., 2025), and flow map methods, including categorical flow maps (CFM) (Roos et al., 2026), flow map language models (FMLM) (Lee et al., 2026a), FMLM with posterior refinement (FMLM+) (Agarwal et al., 2026), and discrete flow maps (DFM) with both the semigroup (PSD) and Eulerian (ESD) objectives (Potaptchik et al., 2026). We evaluate FMLM+ using the released checkpoints with one integration step per refinement round, like DBTM. Baseline values are taken from Lee et al. (2026a); Potaptchik et al. (2026) or evaluated from published checkpoints.

Evaluation Metrics

We report generative perplexity (Gen. PPL) scored by GPT-2 Large (Radford et al., 2019) and sample entropy over 10241024 generated sequences. The goal is to minimize Gen. PPL while maximizing entropy to match the data entropy of LM1B (entropy=4.336\texttt{entropy}{=}4.336) and OWT (entropy=5.441\texttt{entropy}{=}5.441).

15.3 Reasoning Experiment Details

Datasets and Tokenization

Following S-FLM (Deschenaux and Gulcehre, 2026) and FMLM+ (Agarwal et al., 2026), Sudoku puzzles with unique solutions are generated at three difficulties set by clue count (easy 4040, medium 3535, hard 3030), with 48,00048{,}000 train and 2,0002{,}000 held-out puzzles per difficulty. Sudoku uses a 1212-token vocabulary (empty, digits 11-99, row separator, BOS) and a grid is 8181 cells plus 88 separators =89=89 tokens, giving the layout [BOS] puzzle(89) [BOS] solution(89) =180=180 tokens with prompt length 9191 and loss on the solution half. TinyGSM (Liu et al., 2023a) pairs grade-school word problems with Python programs, tokenized by SmolLM-135M (V=49,152V{=}49{,}152) as [BOS] question \n program [EOS] at length 512512, supervising the program region only. Evaluation uses the real GSM8K test set (1,3191{,}319 problems) that was never trained on.

Training Configuration

Sudoku uses the 512512-wide backbone (≈30{\approx}30M parameters) at L=180L{=}180 and TinyGSM the 768768-wide one (≈165{\approx}165M) at L=512L{=}512, with global batch 256256 and 30,00030{,}000 / 50,00050{,}000 warmup steps respectively. Transport-map training matches the language setting (linear interpolant, σ=1.0\sigma{=}1.0, OT coupling, uniform time, clean_context, adaptive transport and cross-entropy endpoint losses, anchor and boundary weights 1.01.0), with tanchor=0.69t_{\text{anchor}}{=}0.69 for Sudoku and tanchor=0.82t_{\text{anchor}}{=}0.82 for TinyGSM. The predictor ϕ\phi is a 256256-wide, 44-layer, 44-head head with quality weight 1.01.0, positive-class reweighting, clean-context labels, and BCE.

Baselines

For the reasoning tasks, we compare DBTM against many-step autoregressive sampling (AR), discrete diffusion methods, including MDLM (Sahoo et al., 2024) and Duo (Sahoo et al., 2025), continuous flow methods, including CANDI (Pynadath et al., 2026), FLM (Lee et al., 2026a), and S-FLM (Deschenaux and Gulcehre, 2026), and the few-step flow map baseline FMLM+ (Agarwal et al., 2026). Baseline values are taken from Agarwal et al. (2026) or evaluated from published checkpoints.

Evaluation Metrics

For Sudoku, we report exact-solve accuracy over the 2,0002{,}000 held-out puzzles. For GSM8K, we report answer accuracy by executing the generated program in a sandbox against the true answer, counting parse or execution failures as incorrect. All numbers use EMA weights and argmax commitment.
